* How a result is checked
=tools/gen-*-oracle.mjs= run Emacs in batch mode and write what it produced; the matching test under =test/= holds the app to it. The files here were made the same way: written, run in Emacs, and the output kept. =test/babel-example.test.js= and =test/examples-emacs.test.js= run them in the app.

#+TITLE: Agenda settings
#+STARTUP: showall
#+CATEGORY: work
#+TODO: TODO NEXT | DONE

Settings that shape the rows of the Agenda: what comes before each heading, the order of the rows, a priority of your own, a Lisp function as a command, how many days show and where they start, finished entries, the log, stuck projects, and commands made of blocks with settings, headers and files of their own. This file is its own sample: the four entries just below are the ones every section lists, for Monday 15 March 2027. Put a setting in Settings → Advanced → *Lisp init*, open this file as an Agenda File, and compare the rows with the ones under each section. The rows are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) showed, and a test in this project checks that the app shows the same. The last section says where the two differ.

* TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-15 Mon 09:00>
:PROPERTIES:
:Effort: 2:00
:WEIGHT: 3
:END:
* TODO Bravo review
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-15 Mon>
:PROPERTIES:
:WEIGHT: 1
:END:
The budget figures are in the spreadsheet.
* NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
DEADLINE: <2027-03-15 Mon>
:PROPERTIES:
:WEIGHT: 2
:END:
* TODO [#B] Delta call <2027-03-15 Mon 11:00>

* The default rows
With nothing set, a row is the category, the time, whether it is scheduled or due, then the heading. Rows go by time of day, then priority, then the order in the file.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "  %-12:c%?-12t% s")))
#+end_src

#+NAME: default
#+begin_example
  work:        9:00...... Scheduled:  TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
  work:       11:00...... TODO [#B] Delta call
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Bravo review
  work:       Deadline:   NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
#+end_example

* What comes before each heading
=org-agenda-prefix-format= is a format string per view. =%c= is the category (=%-8:c= pads it to 8 and adds the colon), =%t= the time, =%s= the scheduling word, =%e= the effort. A =?= makes the part disappear when it is empty.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "%-8:c %?-12t %e ")))
#+end_src

#+NAME: prefix-short
#+begin_example
work:     9:00......  2:00 TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
work:    11:00......   TODO [#B] Delta call
work:      TODO Bravo review
work:      NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
#+end_example

* A Lisp form in the prefix
=%(form)= is evaluated for each row, with =category=, =time=, =level=, =effort= and =tag= set to that row's values; what it returns takes the place of the form.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "%(upcase category) %(concat \"<\" (substring category 0 1) \">\") ")))
#+end_src

#+NAME: prefix-lisp
#+begin_example
WORK <w> TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
WORK <w> TODO [#B] Delta call
WORK <w> TODO Bravo review
WORK <w> NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
#+end_example

* A format that is a plain string
The value may also be one string, used for every view. Emacs reads it as a Lisp string, so =\"= is a quote mark and =\\= a backslash. The time is =%t=: a one-digit hour has a space before it.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format "%-6c \"%t\"%s ")
#+end_src

#+NAME: prefix-string
#+begin_example
work   " 9:00......"Scheduled:  TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
work   "11:00......" TODO [#B] Delta call
work   ""Scheduled:  TODO Bravo review
work   ""Deadline:   NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
#+end_example

* A form that fails
When a =%(form)= fails, the Agenda stops and shows the error in place of the rows.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "%(no-such-function category) %c")))
#+end_src

#+NAME: prefix-error
#+begin_example
Symbol's function definition is void: no-such-function
#+end_example

* A value that cannot be used
A value of the wrong kind stops the Agenda with a message. =org-deadline-warning-days= is a number of days; here it is the symbol =soon=.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "  %-12:c%?-12t% s")))
(setq org-deadline-warning-days 'soon)
#+end_src

#+NAME: unusable-value
#+begin_example
Wrong type argument: number-or-marker-p, soon
#+end_example

* The order of the rows
=org-agenda-sorting-strategy= lists the keys to sort by, per view. Here the highest priority comes first and the rest keep their order in the file.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "  %-12:c%?-12t% s")))
(setq org-agenda-sorting-strategy '((agenda priority-down category-keep)))
#+end_src

#+NAME: sort-priority
#+begin_example
  work:        9:00...... Scheduled:  TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Bravo review
  work:       11:00...... TODO [#B] Delta call
  work:       Deadline:   NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
#+end_example

* Sorting by your own rule
=user-defined-up= and =user-defined-down= sort by =org-agenda-cmp-user-defined=, a function of two agenda lines. It returns =-1= to put the first line first, =1= to put it second, or =nil= for no opinion. This one puts the rows tagged =ops= first.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "  %-12:c%?-12t% s")))
(setq org-agenda-sorting-strategy '((agenda user-defined-up)))
(setq org-agenda-cmp-user-defined (lambda (a b) (cond ((string-match-p ":ops:" a) -1) ((string-match-p ":ops:" b) 1))))
#+end_src

#+NAME: sort-user
#+begin_example
  work:        9:00...... Scheduled:  TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
  work:       Deadline:   NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Bravo review
  work:       11:00...... TODO [#B] Delta call
#+end_example

* A priority of your own
=org-priority-get-priority-function= gives the priority number of a heading, from its text, instead of the letter. It runs with the cursor on the heading, so it can read a property. Here the =WEIGHT= property is the number. A scheduled or due entry still adds its own part to the number, as it does to a letter's.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "  %-12:c%?-12t% s")))
(setq org-agenda-sorting-strategy '((agenda priority-down)))
(setq org-priority-get-priority-function (lambda (headline) (string-to-number (or (org-entry-get nil "WEIGHT") "0"))))
#+end_src

#+NAME: priority-function
#+begin_example
  work:        9:00...... Scheduled:  TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Bravo review
  work:       Deadline:   NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
  work:       11:00...... TODO [#B] Delta call
#+end_example

* Keyword search shows the heading only
A Keyword search finds an entry by its text, not only its heading. The query below is the word in the text of Bravo, written as a regular expression in braces. It finds Bravo, and the row shows the heading alone.

The query is ={bud[g]et}=.

#+NAME: search
#+begin_example
  work:       TODO Bravo review
#+end_example

* Match shows the heading only
The Match query =ops|home= lists the entries with either tag.

The query is =ops|home=.

#+NAME: match
#+begin_example
  work:       TODO [#A] Alpha deploy :ops:
  work:       NEXT [#C] Charlie cleanup :home:
#+end_example

* A function as a command
In =org-agenda-custom-commands=, a command whose type is a function calls it with the command's match string. What the function prints is the result; what it returns is not shown.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-custom-commands '(("x" "Mine" (lambda (match) (princ (format "Report for %s\n" match)) (princ "second line\n") "a result that is not shown") "ops")))
#+end_src

#+NAME: function-command
#+begin_example
Report for ops
second line
#+end_example

* A week of entries
The scenarios from here on use a second sample: the week of Monday 15 March 2027, and two projects for the stuck view. Its entries are in the block below.

#+begin_src org
* TODO Plan sprint
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-15 Mon>
* DONE Ship release
CLOSED: [2027-03-16 Tue 08:30]
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-16 Tue>
* TODO Write report
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-17 Wed 10:00>
* TODO Dentist <2027-03-19 Fri 15:00>
* TODO Review budget
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-20 Sat>
* Website :project:
** NEXT Draft copy
* Garden :project:
** TODO Buy seeds
#+end_src

* The days shown: org-agenda-span
=org-agenda-span= is the number of days the Agenda shows: =day=, =week=, =month=, =year= (a symbol) or a number. A week starts on the day of =org-agenda-start-on-weekday= (1 is Monday; =nil= starts today). Each day has a heading, and the first day of a week carries the week number.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-span 'week)
(setq org-agenda-start-on-weekday 1)
#+end_src

#+NAME: span-week
#+begin_example
Monday     15 March 2027 W11
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Plan sprint
Tuesday    16 March 2027
  work:       DONE Ship release
Wednesday  17 March 2027
  work:       10:00...... Scheduled:  TODO Write report
Thursday   18 March 2027
Friday     19 March 2027
  work:       15:00...... TODO Dentist
Saturday   20 March 2027
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Review budget
Sunday     21 March 2027
#+end_example

* Where the days start: org-agenda-start-day
=org-agenda-start-day= is the first day shown: a date, or an offset from today such as ="+1d"=. With a number of days as the span, the Agenda begins there and does not look for a weekday.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-span 3)
(setq org-agenda-start-day "2027-03-17")
#+end_src

#+NAME: start-day
#+begin_example
Wednesday  17 March 2027
  work:       10:00...... Scheduled:  TODO Write report
Thursday   18 March 2027
Friday     19 March 2027
  work:       15:00...... TODO Dentist
#+end_example

* Hiding finished entries
=org-agenda-skip-scheduled-if-done= leaves out an entry that is done even though it still has a scheduled date; =org-agenda-skip-deadline-if-done= does the same for deadlines. Emacs also lists the scheduled date of a done entry as a plain timestamp, which =org-agenda-skip-timestamp-if-done= leaves out. With both set, Ship release is no longer listed on Tuesday.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-span 'week)
(setq org-agenda-start-on-weekday 1)
(setq org-agenda-skip-scheduled-if-done t)
(setq org-agenda-skip-timestamp-if-done t)
#+end_src

#+NAME: skip-done
#+begin_example
Monday     15 March 2027 W11
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Plan sprint
Tuesday    16 March 2027
Wednesday  17 March 2027
  work:       10:00...... Scheduled:  TODO Write report
Thursday   18 March 2027
Friday     19 March 2027
  work:       15:00...... TODO Dentist
Saturday   20 March 2027
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Review budget
Sunday     21 March 2027
#+end_example

* The log: closed entries
=org-agenda-start-with-log-mode= adds the entries the log records. With =t= every kind is shown: when an entry was closed, state changes and clocked time. Here Ship release shows when it was closed.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-span 'week)
(setq org-agenda-start-on-weekday 1)
(setq org-agenda-start-with-log-mode t)
#+end_src

#+NAME: log-mode
#+begin_example
Monday     15 March 2027 W11
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Plan sprint
Tuesday    16 March 2027
  work:        8:30...... Closed:     DONE Ship release
  work:       DONE Ship release
Wednesday  17 March 2027
  work:       10:00...... Scheduled:  TODO Write report
Thursday   18 March 2027
Friday     19 March 2027
  work:       15:00...... TODO Dentist
Saturday   20 March 2027
  work:       Scheduled:  TODO Review budget
Sunday     21 March 2027
#+end_example

* Stuck projects
=org-stuck-projects= says what a project is and what makes it not stuck: a matcher for the projects, TODO keywords or tags a next action carries, and a regular expression. A project with none of those under it is stuck. Website has a NEXT entry, Garden does not.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-stuck-projects '("+LEVEL=1+project" ("NEXT") nil ""))
#+end_src

#+NAME: stuck
#+begin_example
  work:       Garden :project:
#+end_example

* A stuck command with its own setting
A `stuck` command takes settings of its own after its description, and they apply to that command only. Here =org-stuck-projects= counts a project as stuck unless a child is NEXT or TODO, so Website, whose only child is NEXT, is stuck and Garden, with a TODO child, is not. The heading is Emacs's own.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-custom-commands
      '(("x" "Stuck" stuck "" ((org-stuck-projects '("+LEVEL=1+project" ("TODO") nil ""))))))
#+end_src

#+NAME: command-stuck
#+begin_example
List of stuck projects:
  work:       Website :project:
#+end_example

* An agenda command with its own settings
An `agenda` command can set =org-agenda-span=, =org-agenda-start-day=, =org-deadline-warning-days=, =org-agenda-prefix-format= and the rest for itself: they go over the variables while the command runs. This one shows three days from Tuesday. It opens as a screen of its own, as Emacs opens its own buffer, and its rows have the keys of the Agenda.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-custom-commands
      '(("x" "Three days" agenda "" ((org-agenda-span 3) (org-agenda-start-day "+1d")))))
#+end_src

#+NAME: command-agenda
#+begin_example
3 days-agenda (W11):
Tuesday    16 March 2027
  work:       DONE Ship release
Wednesday  17 March 2027
  work:       10:00...... Scheduled:  TODO Write report
Thursday   18 March 2027
#+end_example

* A composite command: blocks, headers and files
A command made of blocks shows each block under its own heading, with a line of `=` between blocks. The settings after the blocks are the whole command's and go over the variables for every block; a block's own settings come after that and go over those. =org-agenda-overriding-header= replaces a block's heading line, and =org-agenda-files= makes a block list those files only (here =other.org=). The agenda block shows its days, the todo block lists the TODO entries of the sample, and the last block lists the other file. In the app a file is written with its source, as =local:other.org=. The app shows the blocks as one screen, one under the other, with live rows: change a state, set a priority or open the heading as in the Agenda, and an agenda block keeps its own span and day buttons.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-custom-commands
      '(("x" "Day and lists"
         ((agenda "" ((org-agenda-span 'day) (org-agenda-overriding-header "Today")))
          (todo "NEXT" ((org-agenda-overriding-header "Next actions")))
          (tags-todo "garden" ((org-agenda-files '("other.org"))
                               (org-agenda-overriding-header "Garden, from the other file"))))
         ((org-agenda-prefix-format '((agenda . "  %-10c %?-12t") (todo . "  %-10c") (tags . "  %-10c")))))))
#+end_src

The file =other.org= is:

#+begin_src org
#+CATEGORY: home
* TODO Mow the lawn :garden:
SCHEDULED: <2027-03-16 Tue>
* TODO Call the plumber
#+end_src

#+NAME: command-block
#+begin_example
Today
Monday     15 March 2027 W11
  work       TODO Plan sprint

===============================================================================
Next actions
  work      NEXT Draft copy :project::

===============================================================================
Garden, from the other file
  home      TODO Mow the lawn :garden:
#+end_example

* Where the app differs from Emacs
Three things. With a value that cannot be used (the section above), Emacs stops with its own error text; the app says which variable holds the value and what it was, and skips what needed it, and a variable that is not set keeps its default. A file a command names with =org-agenda-files= is written with its source in the app (=local:other.org=, =github:...=, =webdav:...=), where Emacs takes a path. The lines Emacs puts under the heading of a single command ("Press ..." with its keys) are not shown, and the text of a command is not the interactive Agenda: it has no keys.
emacs: Spurious CATEGORY keyword.  Set :CATEGORY: property instead

cases.text:
#+TITLE: Archiving and refiling
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for moving subtrees. Each section shows the files before, and after the operation named under its title; the files live in =/home/me/org= and the clock reads 2026-10-11 16:30. The "after" texts are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) left, and the app gives the same except where the last section says otherwise. Lines that start with =*= or =#+= carry a comma, as org requires inside a block.

* Archive to the default file
With no setting, the subtree goes to a file named like this one with =_archive= added, at the top level. The first line records where it came from; each of the six properties says where the subtree was.

Archive the heading =File taxes=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org_archive:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
#    -*- mode: org -*-


Archived entries from file /home/me/org/notes.org


,* TODO [#A] File taxes                                                  :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Projects
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:ARCHIVE_ITAGS: work
:END:
See the form.
,** Gather receipts
#+END_SRC

* Archive under a heading of the same file
=#+ARCHIVE: ::* Archived Tasks= keeps the subtree in this file, under a heading that is created at the end if it is not there yet.

Archive the heading =File taxes=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: ::* Archived Tasks
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: ::* Archived Tasks
,* Projects :work:
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores

,* Archived Tasks

,** TODO [#A] File taxes                                            :work:tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Projects
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:ARCHIVE_ITAGS: work
:END:
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
#+END_SRC

* Archive to one file, under a heading named after this one
=%s= in the location is the name of the file; the heading is created in the archive file.

Archive the heading =File taxes=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: archive.org::* From %s
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: archive.org::* From %s
,* Projects :work:
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, archive.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org

Archived entries from file /home/me/org/notes.org


,* From notes.org

,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Projects
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:ARCHIVE_ITAGS: work
:END:
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
#+END_SRC

* A heading with its own location
The =ARCHIVE= property of a heading beats the file's =#+ARCHIVE:= line.

Archive the heading =File taxes=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: archive.org::
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO File taxes :tax:
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE: ::* Tax papers
:END:
,** Plan the year
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: archive.org::
,* Projects :work:
,** Plan the year

,* Tax papers

,** TODO File taxes                                                 :work:tax:
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE: ::* Tax papers
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Projects
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:ARCHIVE_ITAGS: work
:END:
#+END_SRC

* Archive a heading with no parent
A top-level heading has no outline path, so =ARCHIVE_OLPATH= and =ARCHIVE_ITAGS= are left out; a property with nothing to say is not written. A heading that is not a TODO has no =ARCHIVE_TODO= either.

Archive the heading =Home=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org_archive:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
#    -*- mode: org -*-


Archived entries from file /home/me/org/notes.org


,* Home
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:END:
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

* Tags and category of the subtree
=ARCHIVE_CATEGORY= is the category the subtree had: its =CATEGORY= property or its parent's, else =#+CATEGORY:=, else the file name. =ARCHIVE_ITAGS= lists the tags it inherited (=#+FILETAGS:= first, then each level from the outermost down; a tag it has itself does not count) separated by spaces. Archived within its own file, the subtree takes those tags on, since it loses its parents.

Archive the heading =Pay=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+CATEGORY: finance
,#+FILETAGS: :office:
,#+ARCHIVE: ::* Done
,* Projects :work:
,** Q4 :money:work:
,*** TODO Pay :tax:money:
,* Done
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+CATEGORY: finance
,#+FILETAGS: :office:
,#+ARCHIVE: ::* Done
,* Projects :work:
,** Q4 :money:work:
,* Done

,** TODO Pay                                           :office:work:tax:money:
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Projects/Q4
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: finance
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:ARCHIVE_ITAGS: office work
:END:
#+END_SRC

* Archive into a heading that has entries
The new entry goes last under the heading, one blank line after what is there.

Archive the heading =Sweep=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: ::* Archived Tasks
,* Home
,** TODO Sweep
,* Archived Tasks
,** DONE Old chore
body
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+ARCHIVE: ::* Archived Tasks
,* Home
,* Archived Tasks
,** DONE Old chore
body

,** TODO Sweep
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Home
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:END:
#+END_SRC

* Archive in place
=C-c C-x a= only adds the =ARCHIVE= tag; the subtree stays where it is, folded, and the agenda leaves it out.

Toggle the archive tag on the heading =Old plan=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO Old plan
body
,** Plan the year
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO Old plan                                                    :ARCHIVE:
body
,** Plan the year
#+END_SRC

* Refile a subtree
The subtree becomes the last child of the target, one level deeper than it, with its own children moved along. Nothing is stamped.

Refile the heading =File taxes= to the heading =Home=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
,** TODO [#A] File taxes                                                 :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
#+END_SRC

* Refile to another file
The same, to a heading of a second file; the first file loses the subtree.

Refile the heading =File taxes= to the heading =Inbox= in =inbox.org=.

Before, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** TODO [#A] File taxes :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

Before, inbox.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Inbox
,** Call Pat
,* Later
#+END_SRC

After, notes.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Projects :work:
,** Plan the year
,* Home
,** Chores
#+END_SRC

After, inbox.org:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Inbox
,** Call Pat
,** TODO [#A] File taxes                                                 :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,*** Gather receipts
,* Later
#+END_SRC

* Restore an archived subtree (the app only)
Org has no command that undoes an archive. *Unarchive* reads the stamps back: the subtree returns to the file and heading named by =ARCHIVE_FILE= and =ARCHIVE_OLPATH=, with its TODO state from =ARCHIVE_TODO= and the stamps removed.

Restore the heading =File taxes= from the archive file.

Before, notes.org_archive:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO [#A] File taxes                                                  :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
:PROPERTIES:
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-10-11 Sun 16:30
:ARCHIVE_FILE: /home/me/org/notes.org
:ARCHIVE_OLPATH: Projects
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: notes
:ARCHIVE_TODO: TODO
:ARCHIVE_ITAGS: work
:END:
See the form.
,** Gather receipts
#+END_SRC

After, restored:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO [#A] File taxes                                                  :tax:
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-20 Tue>
See the form.
,** Gather receipts
#+END_SRC

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- *Restoring* is the app's own command; Org 9.6 has no =org-unarchive-subtree=. It puts the subtree back under the heading named by =ARCHIVE_OLPATH=, at the level that gives, without the stamps and without the tags it took on from its parents.

#+TITLE: Attachments
#+STARTUP: showall

Where a heading keeps its files, and what attaching one writes. The results are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) gave for the outline below, kept in =/home/me/org/notes.org=; the app gives the same where the last section does not say otherwise. Choosing files, the camera and recording are the app's own and are not here.

The outline:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes :work:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: 7a3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
:END:
,** Form 1040
,** Receipts
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: 11223344-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
:END:
,* Trips
:PROPERTIES:
:DIR: files/trips
:END:
,** Packing list
,* Ideas
#+END_SRC

* Where the files go
A heading with an =ID= keeps its files in =data/= with the first two characters of the ID as a folder, and the rest as a folder under it. A =DIR= property names a folder of your choosing, relative to the file. A heading with neither has no folder, and a sub-heading does not use its parent's.

- =Taxes= :: data/7a/3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
- =Form 1040= :: (none)
- =Receipts= :: data/11/223344-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
- =Trips= :: files/trips
- =Packing list= :: (none)
- =Ideas= :: (none)

* Attaching
Attaching a file copies it into the folder and puts the =ATTACH= tag on the heading. The files are listed with their folder; the outline is shown after the last file is attached.

Attach =w2.pdf= to =Taxes=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes                                                         :work:ATTACH:
,** Form 1040
,** Receipts
,* Trips
,** Packing list
,* Ideas
#+END_SRC
Files:
- data/7a/3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d/w2.pdf

Attach =w2.pdf= and =notes.txt= to =Taxes=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes                                                         :work:ATTACH:
,** Form 1040
,** Receipts
,* Trips
,** Packing list
,* Ideas
#+END_SRC
Files:
- data/7a/3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d/notes.txt
- data/7a/3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d/w2.pdf

Attach =ticket.pdf= to =Trips=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes :work:
,** Form 1040
,** Receipts
,* Trips                                                              :ATTACH:
,** Packing list
,* Ideas
#+END_SRC
Files:
- files/trips/ticket.pdf

Attach =my report (final).pdf= and =a?b.txt= to =Taxes=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes                                                         :work:ATTACH:
,** Form 1040
,** Receipts
,* Trips
,** Packing list
,* Ideas
#+END_SRC
Files:
- data/7a/3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d/a?b.txt
- data/7a/3b9c4e-5d6f-4a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d/my report (final).pdf

Attaching a name that is already in the folder stops with "File already exists" and the path, in Emacs and in the app; neither renames or overwrites.

* Deleting
Deleting all the attachments removes the folder and the =ATTACH= tag.

Attach =w2.pdf= and =notes.txt= to =Taxes=, then delete all:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes                                                                :work:
,** Form 1040
,** Receipts
,* Trips
,** Packing list
,* Ideas
#+END_SRC
Files left: (none)

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- *Link text*: attaching can add an =[[attachment:name]]= link to the text (Settings → Attachments); Emacs only adds the tag.

#+TITLE: Emacs Lisp blocks
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for =emacs-lisp= source blocks, which run by default. Use the block's *Run* button (in Emacs, =C-c C-c=). The =#+RESULTS:= under each block is what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) writes for it; the app writes the same text. The last section says where the two differ.

* A value and its layout
A block's last value is laid out by its type: a number is a =: = line, a list of lists is a table, a list of values is a table of one row, and a string is a =: = line.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(* 6 7)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 42

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(list (list 1 2) (list 3 4))
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
| 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 4 |

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :results list
(list 1 2 3)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
- 1
- 2
- 3

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(concat "ab" "cd")
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: abcd

* Output instead of value
=:results output= collects what the code prints.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :results output
(princ "one\n")
(print '(1 "two"))
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: one
: 
: (1 "two")

* Header arguments from the outline
=:header-args:emacs-lisp:= in a property drawer (or =#+PROPERTY: header-args:emacs-lisp= at the top of the file) gives every block below it its arguments, and the block's own header wins. A =:results= word replaces the word of the same kind from above: here the second block takes =value= in place of =output=.

** Printing for the whole subtree
:PROPERTIES:
:header-args:emacs-lisp: :results output
:END:

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(princ (+ 1 2))
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 3

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :results value
(list 1 2)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
| 1 | 2 |

* Variables
=:var= takes a number, a string, or the name of a table, a list, a result or a block anywhere in the file (the first one with that name). A named block is run, and a call such as =triple(n=4)= or =triple(4)= gives its variables. A header row followed by one rule is left out; `name[row,column]` picks a cell, counting from 0.

#+NAME: sales
| quarter | amount |
|---------+--------|
| Q1      |     10 |
| Q2      |     20 |

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var data=sales
(mapcar (lambda (row) (* 2 (cadr row))) data)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
| 20 | 40 |

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var last=sales[-1,1]
last
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 20

#+NAME: ten
#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(* 2 5)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS: ten
: 10

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var n=ten
(+ n 1)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 11

#+NAME: triple
#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var n=1
(* n 3)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS: triple
: 3

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var x=triple(n=4)
x
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 12

#+NAME: shopping
- milk
- eggs
- bread

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var items=shopping
(length items)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 3

#+HEADER: :var x=3
#+begin_src emacs-lisp :var y=4
(* x y)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 12

* Noweb
=:noweb yes= replaces =<<name>>= by the body of the block with that name, before the block runs.

#+NAME: greeting
#+begin_src emacs-lisp :results silent
"hello"
#+end_src

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :noweb yes
(concat <<greeting>> ", world")
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: hello, world

* Wrapping
=:wrap= puts the result in a block of that name; =:results raw= pastes text as Org.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :wrap quote
(+ 1 1)
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
#+begin_quote
2
#+end_quote

#+begin_src emacs-lisp :results raw
"*bold* and /italic/"
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
*bold* and /italic/

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- A heading with an empty =:header-args:= value and a =:header-args+:= line makes Emacs drop the first two characters of the appended arguments (=:tangle yes= becomes =angle yes=); the app appends them as written.
- A block named in a =:var= must be an Emacs Lisp block; Emacs also runs a JavaScript block there.
- Emacs finds a block written inside a =:LOGBOOK:= drawer; the app does not.
- A line that looks like a heading ends the section in Emacs, so a block holding one is not a block there; the app keeps it a block.

#+TITLE: JavaScript blocks
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for =js= source blocks. Turn on *Run JavaScript source blocks* in Settings, then use the block's *Run* button (in Emacs, =C-c C-c= with =(js . t)= in =org-babel-load-languages=). The =#+RESULTS:= under each block is what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) writes for it; the app writes the same text. The last section says where the two differ.

* A value and its layout
A block's =return= value is laid out by its type: a number is a =: = line, an array of arrays is a table, an array of values is a list.

#+begin_src js
return 6 * 7;
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 42

#+begin_src js
return [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
| 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 4 |

#+begin_src js :results list
return [1, 2, 3];
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
- 1
- 2
- 3

* Tables in, tables out
=:var= takes a named table. A header row followed by one rule is left out, as in Org; =:colnames yes= leaves out the first row of a table without a rule, and =:rownames yes= the first column.

#+NAME: sales
| quarter | amount |
|---------+--------|
| Q1      |     10 |
| Q2      |     20 |

#+begin_src js :var data=sales
return data.map(([q, n]) => [q, n * 2]);
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
| Q1 | 20 |
| Q2 | 40 |

Pick a cell or a range with =name[row,column]=; indices count from 0 and from the end when negative, and a rule counts as a row.

#+begin_src js :var last=sales[-1,1]
return last;
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 20

* Output instead of value
=:results output= collects =console.log= lines.

#+begin_src js :results output
console.log('one');
console.log([1, 'two'], { a: 3 });
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: one
: [ 1, 'two' ] { a: 3 }

* Wrapping and other result types
=:results raw= pastes the text as Org; =:wrap= puts the result in a block of that name.

#+begin_src js :results output raw
console.log('*bold* and /italic/');
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
*bold* and /italic/

#+begin_src js :wrap quote
return 42;
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
#+begin_quote
42
#+end_quote

* Around the code
=:prologue= and =:epilogue= put text before and after the code.

#+begin_src js :prologue "const base = 100;" :epilogue "// done"
return base + 1;
#+end_src

#+RESULTS:
: 101

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- Emacs hands a =:results value= string to the Lisp reader, which cuts it at its first space, drops backslashes and refuses =''= or =#=; =:results raw= of =return '*bold*'= comes out as ='*bold*'=. The app keeps the string whole.
- Emacs mixes =console.log= lines into a =:results value= block's result in some versions; the app never does.
- =:hlines yes= passes a rule to the script. Emacs writes the bare word =hline=, which Node cannot run; the app passes the string ="hline"=.
- =:post=, and =file=, =link= and =graphics= results, are not supported.
- A long array or object in =console.log= stays on one line; Node breaks it over several.

#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for journals. Each section shows the file before, the template, and the file after org-capture files it. The results are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) produced, and a test holds the app to them. The template is written the way it goes in the Lisp init (=org-xx-lisp-init=).

* A new day tree
A file+olp+datetree target files under the year, the month and the day of the capture. Headings that are not there yet are made: the year, the month with its name, and the day with its weekday. Here the file is empty.

#+TITLE: Capture templates
#+STARTUP: showall

Capture templates for the Lisp init (=org-xx-lisp-init=, Settings > Advanced), the form Emacs reads, and what they do beyond a fixed place. Each section shows the file before, the Lisp to copy into the init, and the file after org-capture files it. The results are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) produced, and a test holds the app to them.

Two keywords make this possible: =(file+function "file.org" FUNCTION)= as a target, and =:prepare-finalize FUNCTION=. A function is a name, a =(lambda () ...)=, and for =:prepare-finalize= also a list of them; it runs in a text buffer as Emacs's (=point=, =re-search-forward=, =insert=, =flush-lines= ...).

* A shared web page
The template for anything shared in from another app: =entry= (Emacs does not shift the headings of =plain= text), with =:empty-lines 1=. In Emacs, =%a= is the link stored for the page and =%i= the text selected when the capture starts. In the app, sharing a web page fills them: =%a= is the page as a link, =[[address][title]]=, and =%i= the shared text, if any. A web page has a title already, so the title prompt is left blank; the note is typed at =%?=.

* Journal by month and day
A helper, =my-olp-target=, finds or makes the headings of an outline path whose names can be worked out from the date (here the month =2026-11 Nov= and the day =2026-11-08=), and a target function uses it. Two templates share the target: =j= for an =item= and =c= for a =checkitem=, both =:prepend t=, so the newest is first. The headings of November are made by the first capture; the second finds them. The text is typed at =%?=.

Captured on 2026-11-08 Sunday 01:19.

Templates captured, in order: j, c.

In the Lisp init:
#+BEGIN_SRC emacs-lisp
(defun my-olp-target (names)
  "Find or create the outline path NAMES in the file and leave point on its last heading.
A heading that has to be created goes last among its siblings."
  (let ((level 1) (start (point-min)) (end (point-max)))
    (dolist (name names)
      (goto-char start)
      (if (re-search-forward (format "^\\*\\{%d\\} %s[ \t]*$" level (regexp-quote name)) end t)
          (setq start (1+ (match-end 0)))
        (goto-char end)
        (unless (bolp) (insert "\n"))
        (insert (make-string level ?*) " " name "\n")
        (setq start (point)))
      (goto-char start)
      (setq end (if (re-search-forward (format "^\\*\\{1,%d\\} " level) nil t) (match-beginning 0) (point-max)))
      (setq level (1+ level)))
    (goto-char start) (forward-line -1) (beginning-of-line)))

(defun my-journal-target ()
  "The day of today in the month of today in the journal."
  (my-olp-target (list "📔 Journal - journal and diary"
                       (format-time-string "%Y-%m %b")
                       (format-time-string "%Y-%m-%d"))))

(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("j" "Journal" item (file+function "journal.org" my-journal-target) "%<%H:%M> - %?" :prepend t))
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("c" "Journal check item" checkitem (file+function "journal.org" my-journal-target) "%?" :prepend t))
#+END_SRC

(defun my-year-heading ()
  "Find or create the heading of this year and leave point on it."
  (let ((year (format-time-string "%Y")))
    (goto-char (point-min))
    (unless (re-search-forward (format "^\\* %s\\(?: .*\\)?$" (regexp-quote year)) nil t)
      (goto-char (point-max))
      (unless (bolp) (insert "\n"))
      (insert "* " year "\n")
      (forward-line -1))
    (beginning-of-line)))

* Tracking
A =table-line= template whose target function finds or makes the headings =Bag=, =Health=, =Tracking= and the current month, puts the new month first, and gives it a plot line, a table and the formulas. The row is filed into that table, the formulas are worked out again, and =:jump-to-captured t= opens the table and scrolls to the new row. The file already has October; two rows are captured in November.

Emacs does not expand =@#= in a template, so the first column is a formula, =$1=@#-1= (the header row counts as a row). Emacs rejects a =#+TBLFM= line that defines =$4== twice ("Double definition"), so one formula gives the hour column.

#+BEGIN_SRC emacs-lisp
(defun my-tracking-target ()
  "Find or create Bag > Health > Tracking > this month and leave point on that heading.
A new heading goes first among its siblings; a new month also gets the plot, the table and its formulas."
  (let ((level 1) (start (point-min)) (end (point-max)))
    (dolist (name (list "🛍️ Bag - lists and notes" "❤️ Health" "🏩 Tracking" (format-time-string "%Y-%m")))
      (goto-char start)
      (if (re-search-forward (format "^\\*\\{%d\\} %s[ \t]*$" level (regexp-quote name)) end t)
          (setq start (1+ (match-end 0)))
        (goto-char start)
        (goto-char (if (re-search-forward "^\\*+ " end t) (match-beginning 0) end))
        (unless (bolp) (insert "\n"))
        (insert (make-string level ?*) " " name "\n")
        (when (= level 4)
          (insert "#+PLOT: title:\"Tracking\" ind:4 deps:1 with:points ticks:6\n|   |\n|---|\n"
                  "#+TBLFM: $1=@#-1 :: $4=if(round(trunc($3/100) + 100*($3/100 - trunc($3/100)) / 60) == 24, 0, round(trunc($3/100) + 100*($3/100 - trunc($3/100)) / 60))\n"))
        (setq start (save-excursion (re-search-backward (format "^\\*\\{%d\\} " level)) (forward-line 1) (point))))
      (goto-char start)
      (setq end (if (re-search-forward (format "^\\*\\{1,%d\\} " level) nil t) (match-beginning 0) (point-max)))
      (setq level (1+ level)))
    (goto-char start) (forward-line -1) (beginning-of-line)))

(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("t" "Tracking" table-line (file+function "github:home.org" my-tracking-target)
     "| | %<%Y-%m-%d> | %<%H%M> ||"
     :jump-to-captured t))
#+END_SRC

* Under today's date
=file+olp+datetree= files a capture under the year, the month and the day, making the headings it needs; =:tree-type week= or =:tree-type month= chooses the week or month tree, and =:prepend t= puts the entry first. =capture-datetree.org= shows each with the file before and after.

* Where the app differs from Emacs
=:before-finalize= runs on the text of the capture, after =:prepare-finalize=, where Emacs runs it on the whole file. =:after-finalize= runs once the entry is filed, in a buffer with no text; =:refile-targets= has no effect. =:clock-in= clocks the new entry when the capture is filed; Emacs does it when the capture buffer opens. A target function may only insert whole lines; one that changes or deletes a line is refused with a message and nothing is filed. A =file+function= template of type =item=, =checkitem= or =table-line= needs the function to leave point on a heading. In the buffer of a function, markers and text properties are not available, the regexp operator ~\=~ never matches, and a search with a bound treats ~$~ and ~\'~ at the bound as the end of the text. The =github:= prefix of a file name is the app's own.

#+TITLE: Citations
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for citations. Point =#+BIBLIOGRAPHY:= at a file (=refs.bib= beside these examples) and write =[cite:@key]=. The LaTeX that Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) writes for each text is shown, the part between =\begin{document}= and =\end{document}=, and the app writes the same. The =basic= processor, which is the default, writes the citation as text and the reference list as paragraphs; =natbib= and =biblatex= write commands for LaTeX to resolve. The last section says where the app differs from Emacs.

* A citation and its list
The default style is author and year. =#+PRINT_BIBLIOGRAPHY:= marks where the reference list goes.

#+begin_src org
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
See [cite:@knuth84] and [cite:@knuth84;@lamport94].

,* References
,#+PRINT_BIBLIOGRAPHY:
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
See (Donald E. Knuth, 1984) and (Donald E. Knuth, 1984, Leslie Lamport and Donald E. Knuth, 1994).

\section{References}
\label{sec:org0000002}
\noindent
Donald E. Knuth (1984). \emph{The {TeX}book}, Addison-Wesley.

\noindent
Leslie Lamport and Donald E. Knuth (1994). \emph{LaTeX: A Document Preparation System}, Journal of Typesetting.
#+end_src

* Styles
=/t= is the text style, =/na= leaves the author out, =/b= is the bare form, and =/n= prints nothing.

#+begin_src org
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
[cite/t:@knuth84], [cite/na:@knuth84], [cite/b:@knuth84], [cite/n:@three].
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
Donald E. Knuth (1984), (1984), (Donald E. Knuth, 1984),.
#+end_src

* Prefix, suffix and page numbers
Text before a key is its prefix, and text after it is its suffix.

#+begin_src org
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
Details in [cite:see @knuth84, p. 5] and [cite/t:@lamport94, chapter 2].
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
Details in (see Donald E. Knuth, 1984, p. 5) and Leslie Lamport and Donald E. Knuth (1994, chapter 2).
#+end_src

* Several authors
The basic processor shortens a long author list.

#+begin_src org
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
Prior work: [cite:@three].

,#+PRINT_BIBLIOGRAPHY:
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
Prior work: (Ann Alpha and Bob Beta and Cy Gamma, 2001).

\noindent
Ann Alpha and Bob Beta and Cy Gamma (2001). \emph{Three authors}.
#+end_src

* natbib
=#+CITE_EXPORT: natbib= leaves the work to LaTeX: =\citep{}=, =\citet{}= and a =\bibliography{}= line. The style after the processor name becomes =\bibliographystyle{}=.

#+begin_src org
,#+CITE_EXPORT: natbib plain
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
See [cite:@knuth84], [cite/t:@lamport94] and [cite/a:@knuth84].

,#+PRINT_BIBLIOGRAPHY:
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
See \citep{knuth84}, \citet{lamport94} and \citeauthor{knuth84}.

\bibliographystyle{plain}
\bibliography{refs}
#+end_src

* biblatex
=#+CITE_EXPORT: biblatex= writes =\autocite{}=, =\textcite{}= and =\printbibliography=.

#+begin_src org
,#+CITE_EXPORT: biblatex
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
See [cite:@knuth84], [cite/t:@lamport94] and [cite/a:@knuth84].

,#+PRINT_BIBLIOGRAPHY:
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
See \autocite{knuth84}, \textcite{lamport94} and \citeauthor*{knuth84}.

\printbibliography
#+end_src

* The author alone
=/a= (the author alone) prints the author in HTML and plain text, but Org 9.6.15's LaTeX export stops with an error; the app stops with the same one.

#+begin_src org
,#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib
,* Notes
By [cite/a:@knuth84].
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
ERROR Wrong type argument: characterp, raw

#+TITLE: Clock tables
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for =#+BEGIN: clocktable=. In Emacs, =C-c C-c= on a block writes the table under it. In the app, *Clock* in the TODO view shows the same table read-only for a date range and any of the parameters in the *Parameters* field. The table under each block here is what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) wrote, and the app's table is the same, apart from the time in the caption, which is when it was made. The last section says where the two differ.

* Projects
** Website
*** Design :ui:
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-08-03 Mon 09:00]--[2026-08-03 Mon 11:30] =>  2:30
CLOCK: [2026-08-04 Tue 14:00]--[2026-08-04 Tue 15:15] =>  1:15
:END:
*** Build
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-08-04 Tue 09:00]--[2026-08-04 Tue 12:00] =>  3:00
:END:
** Taxes :money:
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-08-05 Wed 10:00]--[2026-08-05 Wed 10:45] =>  0:45
:END:

* The week, two levels deep
=:tstart= is included and =:tend= is not. A parent row includes its children.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2 :scope file :tstart "2026-08-03" :tend "2026-08-10"
#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
| Headline     | Time   |      |
|--------------+--------+------|
| *Total time* | *7:30* |      |
|--------------+--------+------|
| Projects     | 7:30   |      |
| \_  Website  |        | 6:45 |
| \_  Taxes    |        | 0:45 |
#+END:

* Only the first day, all levels
#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 4 :scope file :tstart "2026-08-04" :tend "2026-08-05"
#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
| Headline     | Time   |      |      |
|--------------+--------+------+------|
| *Total time* | *4:15* |      |      |
|--------------+--------+------+------|
| Projects     | 4:15   |      |      |
| \_  Website  |        | 4:15 |      |
| \_    Design |        |      | 1:15 |
| \_    Build  |        |      | 3:00 |
#+END:

* A block: a whole month
=:block 2026-08= is the month; =2026-W32= is a week and =2026-08-04= a day. =today=, =thisweek= and =lastmonth= work too.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2 :scope file :block 2026-08
#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30], for August 2026.
| Headline     | Time   |      |
|--------------+--------+------|
| *Total time* | *7:30* |      |
|--------------+--------+------|
| Projects     | 7:30   |      |
| \_  Website  |        | 6:45 |
| \_  Taxes    |        | 0:45 |
#+END:

* A step: one table per week
=:step week= with a range writes a table for each week, headed by its dates.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2 :scope file :tstart "2026-08-03" :tend "2026-08-17" :step week

Weekly report starting on: [2026-08-03 Mon]
| Headline     | Time   |      |
|--------------+--------+------|
| *Total time* | *7:30* |      |
|--------------+--------+------|
| Projects     | 7:30   |      |
| \_  Website  |        | 6:45 |
| \_  Taxes    |        | 0:45 |

Weekly report starting on: [2026-08-10 Mon]
| Headline     | Time   |
|--------------+--------|
| *Total time* | *0:00* |
#+END:

* Only headings with a tag
=:match= takes a tag match, as in the Agenda.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 4 :scope file :block 2026-08 :match "money|ui"
#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30], for August 2026.
| Headline     | Time   |      |      |
|--------------+--------+------+------|
| *Total time* | *4:30* |      |      |
|--------------+--------+------+------|
| Projects     | 4:30   |      |      |
| \_  Website  |        | 3:45 |      |
| \_    Design |        |      | 3:45 |
| \_  Taxes    |        | 0:45 |      |
#+END:

* Percent of the total
=:formula %= adds a column with each row's share of the total.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2 :scope file :block 2026-08 :formula %
#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30], for August 2026.
| Headline     | Time   |      |     % |
|--------------+--------+------+-------|
| *Total time* | *7:30* |      | 100.0 |
|--------------+--------+------+-------|
| Projects     | 7:30   |      | 100.0 |
| \_  Website  |        | 6:45 |  90.0 |
| \_  Taxes    |        | 0:45 |  10.0 |
#+END:

* Links and a compact table
=:link t= makes the headlines links to the headings; =:compact t= puts all the times in one column.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2 :scope file :block 2026-08 :link t :compact t
#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30], for August 2026.
| Headline     |   Time |
|--------------+--------|
| *Total time* | *7:30* |
|--------------+--------|
| [[file:/home/me/org/clock-tables.org::*Projects][Projects]]     |   7:30 |
| \_  [[file:/home/me/org/clock-tables.org::*Website][Website]]  |   6:45 |
| \_  [[file:/home/me/org/clock-tables.org::*Taxes][Taxes]]    |   0:45 |
#+END:

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- The app does not write the table into the file: it shows it in the TODO view. Open this file, pick *Clock*, and give the dates and the parameters.
- The caption time is the time of the update, as Emacs writes it.

#+TITLE: Column view
#+STARTUP: showall
#+COLUMNS: %30ITEM(Task) %TODO %10Effort(Estimate){:} %CLOCKSUM(Spent) %Cost(Cost){+;%.2f}

Column view shows headings as table rows and properties as columns. Open the command palette and choose *Column view* (C-c C-x C-c) with the cursor on a heading to see that subtree, or above the first heading to see the whole file. Tap a cell to change it. The columns come from the =#+COLUMNS:= line above, and a =:COLUMNS:= property on a heading replaces them for its subtree. Parent rows show the sum of their children (=Estimate= as hours, =Cost= with two decimals).

* Website relaunch

:COST:     2096.50
:END:
** TODO Design

:Cost: 1200
:END:
:LOGBOOK:

:END:

:Cost: 800.5
:END:
*** TODO Templates

:PROPERTIES:

:END:

:Cost: 96

* Another view of the same data
:PROPERTIES:
:COLUMNS: %25ITEM %TODO %Cost(Cost){min} %Cost(Mean){mean}
:END:
This heading has its own =:COLUMNS:= property: the cheapest and the average cost of the entries below it, instead of the sum. The block below is made from this heading (=:id local=), so it uses that format.

#+BEGIN: columnview :id local
| ITEM                          | TODO | Cost | Mean |
|-------------------------------+------+------+------|
| Another view of the same data |      |   10 | 20.0 |
| One                           |      |   10 |   10 |
| Two                           |      |   30 |   30 |

:PROPERTIES:

** Two

* A dynamic block
A =columnview= block is a table that is written into the file, to read or export. =org-update-dblock= (C-c C-x C-u) on the block, or =org-update-all-dblocks= for the file, writes it again. Here =:id= names the heading it is made from, =:hlines 1= puts a line under the first level, =:skip-empty-rows t= leaves out rows with nothing in the columns, and =:maxlevel 2= stops at the second level.

#+BEGIN: columnview :id global :hlines 1 :maxlevel 2
| Task                          | TODO | Estimate | Spent |    Cost |
|-------------------------------+------+----------+-------+---------|
| Website relaunch              |      | 2d 7:00  |  4:15 | 2096.50 |
| Design                        | TODO | 6:00     |  3:30 | 1200.00 |
| Build                         | TODO | 2d 0:00  |       |  800.50 |
| Hosting                       | DONE | 1:00     |  0:45 |   96.00 |

|-------------------------------+------+----------+-------+---------|
| A dynamic block               |      |          |       |    0.00 |
| Only the entries that match   |      |          |       |    0.00 |
#+END:

#+BEGIN: columnview :id global :match "TODO=\"TODO\"" :skip-empty-rows t

#+TITLE: Org Crypt
#+STARTUP: showall

Org Crypt keeps the text of an entry secret in the file: it is replaced by a block of =-----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----= text that Emacs (=org-decrypt-entry=) and gpg can open too. The heading, its tags and its properties stay readable. Everything below them, sub-headings included, is encrypted.

Open the command palette and choose:
- *Encrypt entry* / *Decrypt entry* (=org-encrypt-entry=, =org-decrypt-entry=): the entry you are on.
- *Encrypt all crypt entries* / *Decrypt all crypt entries* (=org-encrypt-entries=, =org-decrypt-entries=): every entry with the =crypt= tag.

The passphrase of every entry in this file is =example=. It is asked for once and kept in memory for ten minutes. While entries are decrypted, the copy of the file kept on this device is not updated (Settings → =org-crypt-disable-auto-save=); save the file after encrypting it again.

The =CRYPTKEY= property of the last entry names the key it is encrypted to; without it, =org-crypt-key= in Settings is used, and without a key, a passphrase. To open that entry, import =crypt-example-key.asc= under Settings → Encryption keys (its passphrase is also =example=), then choose *Decrypt entry*. It is a key for trying this out; do not use it for anything real.

#+TITLE: Diary
#+STARTUP: showall

The diary is a plain text file of dated lines. Each line says "on this day, show this", and the Agenda lists the lines that fall on each day, with that day's holidays. It is Emacs's own diary, so a diary file written for Emacs works here as it is.

* Turn it on
Set two things in Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → *Diary*: tick *Include the diary file in the Agenda* (=org-agenda-include-diary=) and give the file in =diary-file= (=github:diary=, =webdav:diary= or =local:diary=). Or put both in the Lisp init (Settings → Advanced):

#+begin_example
(setq org-agenda-include-diary t
      diary-file "github:diary")
#+end_example

Settings the Lisp init sets are shown in Settings marked "Set by the Lisp init". *Refresh* in the Agenda reads the diary again after you edit it.

* The example diary
=examples/diary= holds the file below. Copy it into your own diary file and open the Agenda to see it.

#+begin_example
# Lines that start with "#" are not entries, so they can be used for notes.
# A line is an entry when it starts with a date; indented lines continue it.

# One day
Nov 12, 2026  9:30am Dentist, 123 Main St
   Bring the insurance card
10/30/2026  4:00pm Call Alex
1/15/2027  Passport renewal due

# Every year
4/20  Tax preparation starts
&12/24  Wrap the presents
%%(diary-anniversary 5 14 1990) Maria's birthday (%d)

# Every week
Monday  7:30am Gym
Fri  Back up the laptop

# Every month
*/1  Rent due
*/15  Payday
%%(= (calendar-extract-day date) (calendar-last-day-of-month (calendar-extract-month date) (calendar-extract-year date))) Last day of the month: send the timesheet

# Patterns Lisp makes easy
%%(diary-float t 1 1) Planning meeting (first Monday)
%%(diary-float 11 4 4) Family dinner (fourth Thursday of November)
%%(diary-block 12 21 2026 1 3 2027) Office closed
%%(diary-cyclic 14 10 26 2026) Trash day (every 14 days)
%%(and (= (calendar-extract-day date) 13) (= (calendar-day-of-week date) 5)) Friday the 13th
%%(diary-remind '(diary-date 6 1 2027) 3) Anniversary dinner
#+end_example

** How the lines are read
- A line that starts with a date is an entry. Indented lines after it belong to it (=Nov 12, 2026= above has a second line).
- Dates are written in the order of =calendar-date-style= (American by default: month, day, year). =*= means any: =*/15= is the 15th of every month. A weekday name (=Monday=, =Fri=) is every week.
- A time at the start of an entry (=9:30am=, =14:30=) puts it in the day's timeline.
- A =&= before the date is a non-marking entry: it shows in the Agenda but would not mark the day in Emacs's calendar window.
- A line that starts =%%(= is a Lisp expression, evaluated once for each day. When it gives a value other than =nil= the entry is listed that day, and if the value is a string, the string is the text. The variable =date= is the day, as =(month day year)=.
- Lines that start with =#=, or anything else that does not begin like a date, are ignored.

** What the Agenda shows
These are what Emacs 29.3 lists for the example file, and what the app lists. A line without a time joins the row before it.

| Day | Rows |
|---+---|
| Fri Oct 30, 2026 | =4:00pm Call Alex; Back up the laptop= |
| Thu Nov 12, 2026 | the day's holiday, then =9:30am Dentist, 123 Main St; Bring the insurance card= |
| Mon Nov 2, 2026 | =Planning meeting (first Monday)=, =7:30am Gym= |
| Mon Oct 26 and Nov 9, 2026 | =Trash day (every 14 days)=, =7:30am Gym= |
| Thu Nov 26, 2026 | =Thanksgiving=, =Family dinner (fourth Thursday of November)= |
| Fri Nov 13, 2026 | =Friday the 13th; Back up the laptop= |
| Mon Nov 30, 2026 | =Last day of the month: send the timesheet=, =7:30am Gym= |
| Fri May 14, 2027 | =Maria's birthday (37); Back up the laptop= |
| Sat May 29, 2027 | =Reminder: Only 3 days until Anniversary dinner= |
| Tue Jun 1, 2027 | =Anniversary dinner; Rent due= |

* Lisp in the diary
Each =%%(...)= line is Emacs Lisp. Besides the diary's own functions (=diary-float=, =diary-block=, =diary-cyclic=, =diary-anniversary=, =diary-remind=, =diary-date=) you can use =let=, =if=, =cond=, =and=, =or=, =setq=, =defun=, loops, lists and =format=:

#+begin_example
%%(let ((n (- (calendar-absolute-from-gregorian '(12 25 2026)) (calendar-absolute-from-gregorian date)))) (and (>= n 0) (<= n 30) (format "%d days until Christmas" n)))
%%(and (= (calendar-day-of-week date) 5) (= (% (calendar-extract-day date) 2) 0) "Even-dated Friday")
#+end_example

A line that fails shows Emacs's message in the Agenda instead of the entry, for example =Symbol’s function definition is void: no-such-function=, and a line that loops forever stops with a message too.

* Diary or calendar?
Three places can hold a date. They are good at different things:

| | Diary file | Org headings with timestamps | A calendar app |
|---+---+---+---|
| An entry is | one line of text | a heading with a state, notes and a clock | an event with a time, place and guests |
| Best for | rules: every third Thursday, 14 days from the 26th, the last day of the month, anniversaries with an age | things you do: a task with =SCHEDULED:= or =DEADLINE:=, a project, a meeting with notes | things other people share: invitations, shared calendars, alerts on your phone |
| Repeats | by any rule Lisp can state | =+1w=, =++1m=, =.+1d= from the date | the app's own repeat rules |
| Done / not done | no | yes (=TODO= and =DONE=) | no |
| Alerts | no | no | yes |
| Other people | no | no | yes |

Some guidance:
- Use the *diary* for the dates that are facts about the calendar: birthdays and anniversaries, holidays of your own, pay days, "first Monday", "every 14 days". One line, no heading, and a rule that Lisp can compute (=diary-float=, =diary-cyclic=).
- Use *Org timestamps* for work you track: anything you mark done, clock, or write notes under. A repeating task whose next date moves when you finish it (=+1w=) belongs here, not in the diary.
- Use a *calendar app* for events that involve other people or need an alert on your phone. The Agenda can be exported as an =.ics= file for one (see =icalendar.org=), so your own dates can show there as well.
- The three mix: a diary line for the trash day, a TODO with a deadline for the report, and a calendar invitation for the dinner all appear together in the Agenda.

* Where the app differs from Emacs
The Coptic, Ethiopic, Persian, French and Mayan date functions are not available. The dates and rows above, and the whole example file, are checked against Emacs 29.3 for 2026 and 2027.

#+TITLE: Editing headings, lists and tables
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for structure edits. Each section shows text before an edit and after it. The "after" texts are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) left (promote and demote with =M-left= and =M-right= on a subtree, =M-up=, =M-RET=, =C-c C-x C-b=, the table commands), and the app gives the same. Lines that start with =*= or =#+= carry a comma, as org requires inside a block.

* Promote a heading
The stars drop by one and the heading stays where it is in the text, so the siblings after it become its children.

Before (promote at line 3):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* A
,** B
,** C
,** D
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* A
,** B
,* C
,** D
#+END_SRC

* Demote a heading
The heading and its subtree go one level deeper. After a sibling it becomes that sibling's last child.

Before (demote at line 3):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* A
,** B
,** C
,*** C1
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* A
,** B
,*** C
,**** C1
#+END_SRC

* Move a subtree
A heading changes places with its sibling, subtree and all.

Before (up at line 3):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* A
,** B
,* C
,** C1
,* D
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* C
,** C1
,* A
,** B
,* D
#+END_SRC

* A new numbered item
Ordered items are numbered again.

Before (item-below at line 3):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Steps
1. Mix
2. Bake
3. Cool
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Steps
1. Mix
2. Bake
3. 
4. Cool
#+END_SRC

* A new item above sub-items
The new item goes right under the item's first line, and the sub-items follow it.

Before (item-below at line 2):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Shopping
- Fruit
  - apples
  - pears
- Bread
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Shopping
- Fruit
- 
  - apples
  - pears
- Bread
#+END_SRC

* A new description item
The term is empty, ready to be filled in.

Before (item-below at line 2):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Terms
- org :: outliner
- pwa :: web app
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Terms
- org :: outliner
-  :: 
- pwa :: web app
#+END_SRC

* Checking a box
A box that has boxes under it shows what they add up to, and the cookie follows.

Before (toggle at line 3):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Packing [0/2]
- [-] Bag [1/2]
  - [ ] shirts
  - [X] shoes
- [ ] Passport
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Packing [1/2]
- [X] Bag [2/2]
  - [X] shirts
  - [X] shoes
- [ ] Passport
#+END_SRC

* Insert a table column
The table is aligned again and the =#+TBLFM:= references move with the columns.

Before (insert-col at line 3, column 2):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
| a | b |
|---+---|
| 1 | 2 |
,#+TBLFM: $2=$1*2
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
| a |   | b |
|---+---+---|
| 1 |   | 2 |
,#+TBLFM: $3=$1*2
#+END_SRC

* Delete a table row
The other rows keep their layout, and row references in =#+TBLFM:= follow.

Before (delete-row at line 3):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
| n | sq |
|---+----|
| 1 |  1 |
| 2 |  4 |
| 3 |  9 |
,#+TBLFM: @4$2=@3$1*@3$1
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
| n | sq |
|---+----|
| 2 |  4 |
| 3 |  9 |
,#+TBLFM: @3$2=@2$1*@2$1
#+END_SRC

* Change a table cell
The columns are widened to the longest cell.

Before (set-cell at line 3, column 1, value "a much longer name"):
#+BEGIN_SRC org
| Name | Qty |
|------+-----|
| ab   |   3 |
#+END_SRC

After:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
| Name               | Qty |
|--------------------+-----|
| a much longer name |   3 |
#+END_SRC

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- Emacs re-aligns a heading's tags to =org-tags-column= when its level changes; the app leaves their spacing as it is.
- Deleting a table column leaves an extra column in Emacs when a row has an empty cell and the rule is a bare =|-=; the app deletes the column asked for.
- A new item below an item with a checkbox has none, as in Emacs; the item menu has *Add checkbox below* for one with a box.

#+TITLE: LaTeX export
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for the LaTeX export (=C-c C-e l l= in Emacs, More → Export → LaTeX in the app). Each section shows an Org text, the settings it needs, and the body of the =.tex= file Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) wrote for it, the part between =\begin{document}= and =\end{document}=. The app writes the same text. Label hashes (=sec:org…=) are numbered by first use, as they differ on every run. Settings go in Settings → Export → LaTeX, in the Lisp box. The last section says where the app differs from Emacs.

* A macro with a template
A =#+MACRO:= is replaced by its text; =$1=, =$2= are the arguments.

#+begin_src org
,#+MACRO: version 1.2
,#+MACRO: greet Hello, $1!
,* Notes
Release {{{version}}}. {{{greet(world)}}}
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
Release 1.2. Hello, world!
#+end_src

* A macro that runs Lisp
A template that starts with =(eval= is evaluated. The arguments are strings, and what the form returns is written as text. An error stops the export.

#+begin_src org
,#+MACRO: gnustamp (eval (concat "GNU/" (capitalize $1)))
,#+MACRO: plural (eval (if (equal $1 "1") (concat $1 " file") (concat $1 " files")))
,* Notes
Running {{{gnustamp(linux)}}} on {{{plural(1)}}}, then {{{plural(3)}}}.
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Notes}
\label{sec:org0000001}
Running GNU/Linux on 1 file, then 3 files.
#+end_src

* Headlines
A TODO keyword and tags are written as =ox-latex= writes them, the tags at the right of the title. A priority shows only with =pri:t=.

#+begin_src org
,#+OPTIONS: pri:t
,* TODO [#A] Write the report :work:urgent:
,** DONE Outline
,* Plain heading
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{{\bfseries\sffamily TODO} \framebox{\#A} Write the report\hfill{}\textsc{work:urgent}}
\label{sec:org0000001}
\subsection{{\bfseries\sffamily DONE} Outline}
\label{sec:org0000002}
\section{Plain heading}
\label{sec:org0000003}
#+end_src

* Leaving the keyword, priority and tags out
=todo:nil=, =pri:t= and =tags:nil= in =#+OPTIONS:= choose what a headline shows.

#+begin_src org
,#+OPTIONS: todo:nil pri:t tags:nil
,* TODO [#B] Write the report :work:
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{\framebox{\#B} Write the report}
\label{sec:org0000001}
#+end_src

* Choosing what is exported
=tasks:todo= keeps only the unfinished TODO headings (the DONE one goes), =arch:nil= drops archived subtrees and =d:nil= drops drawers. Every key =#+OPTIONS:= takes is listed in the README.

#+begin_src org
,#+OPTIONS: tasks:todo arch:nil d:nil
,* TODO Open
The meeting runs long.
:LOGBOOK:
- Note taken
:END:
,* DONE Closed
closed text
,* Old :ARCHIVE:
hidden
,* Plain
stays
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{{\bfseries\sffamily TODO} Open}
\label{sec:org0000001}
The meeting runs long.
\section{Plain}
\label{sec:org0000002}
stays
#+end_src

* Your own headline format
=org-latex-format-headline-function= is called for every section title and low-level list headline with the keyword, its type (=todo= or =done=), the priority as a character code, the title, the tags and the export info. Whatever it returns is the headline.

#+begin_src org
,* TODO Write the report :work:
,* Read the notes
#+end_src

Settings:

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-latex-format-headline-function
      (lambda (todo todo-type priority text tags info)
        (concat (if todo (format "[%s] " todo) "")
                text
                (if tags (concat " #" (mapconcat #'identity tags ",")) ""))))
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{[TODO] Write the report #work}
\label{sec:org0000001}
\section{Read the notes}
\label{sec:org0000002}
#+end_src

* A named headline function
A function you define can be given by name.

#+begin_src org
,* TODO Open task
,* DONE Finished task
#+end_src

Settings:

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(defun my-headline (todo todo-type priority text tags info)
  (if (eq todo-type (quote done))
      (concat "\\sout{" text "}")
    text))
(setq org-latex-format-headline-function #'my-headline)
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section{Open task}
\label{sec:org0000001}
\section{\sout{Finished task}}
\label{sec:org0000002}
#+end_src

* A different class
=org-latex-classes= defines a class and its sectioning commands. =#+LATEX_CLASS:= picks it for one file.

#+begin_src org
,#+LATEX_CLASS: memo
,* To the team
,** Schedule
We meet on Friday.
#+end_src

Settings:

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(add-to-list 'org-latex-classes
  '("memo" "\\documentclass{article}"
    ("\\section*{%s}" . "\\section*{%s}")
    ("\\subsection*{%s}" . "\\subsection*{%s}")))
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\section*{To the team}
\label{sec:org0000001}
\subsection*{Schedule}
\label{sec:org0000002}
We meet on Friday.
#+end_src

* A table with attributes
=#+ATTR_LATEX:= sets the column alignment, the table environment and booktabs rules.

#+begin_src org
,#+CAPTION: Prices
,#+ATTR_LATEX: :align lrr :booktabs t
| Item | Price | Qty |
|------+-------+-----|
| Pen  |  1.50 |   4 |
| Book | 12.00 |   2 |
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\begin{table}[htbp]
\caption{Prices}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Item & Price & Qty\\[0pt]
\midrule
Pen & 1.50 & 4\\[0pt]
Book & 12.00 & 2\\[0pt]
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
#+end_src

* A figure
A link to an image with a caption becomes a =figure=. =:width= and =:placement= go in =#+ATTR_LATEX:=.

#+begin_src org
,#+CAPTION: A cat
,#+NAME: fig-cat
,#+ATTR_LATEX: :width 0.5\textwidth :placement [h]
[[file:cat.png]]

See [[fig-cat]].
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{cat.png}
\caption{\label{fig:org0000001}A cat}
\end{figure}

See \ref{fig:org0000001}.
#+end_src

* A link to a figure by name
A link whose target is the =#+NAME:= of a figure, even a name with a colon, is a reference to it.

#+begin_src org
,#+CAPTION: A cat
,#+NAME: fig:cat
[[file:cat.png]]

See [[fig:cat]].
#+end_src

Emacs writes:

#+begin_src latex
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.9\linewidth]{cat.png}
\caption{\label{fig:org0000001}A cat}
\end{figure}

See \ref{fig:org0000001}.
#+end_src

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- =org-latex-format-headline-function= is called with =nil= in place of the export info, so a function that reads it sees nothing.
- A macro =(eval ..)= runs on the app's own Lisp interpreter (see the Lisp init), not on Emacs, so a function the interpreter does not have gives an error.

#+TITLE: God-mode
#+STARTUP: showall
#+TODO: TODO NEXT | DONE

God-mode reaches Org's full key set (=C-c C-t=, =M-RET= and the rest) without a held Ctrl or Alt key. Every key you press is read as part of a sequence, and a card under the top bar lists the keys that can come next, as Emacs's which-key does. Tap a key on the card to send it, so a whole chord can be done with no keyboard at all.

* Start and stop
| To | Do |
|---+---|
| Turn it on | Press =Escape=, or on a phone tap the floating *[g]* button (it also shows a keyboard of its own) |
| Turn it off | =Escape= again |
| Cancel a half-typed sequence | =Escape= (the card goes away) |

The minibuffer at the bottom echoes what you type and, when a sequence is done, names what ran: =God-mode · C-c C-x C-j → Go to clocked task=. Opening a panel (Settings, Search, a menu) turns god-mode off.

* The rules
- A plain key means Control: =t= is =C-t=.
- =g= puts Meta on the next key: =g↑= is =M-↑=. (So a bare =C-g= cannot be typed.) =G= (Shift+g) is Control and Meta: =Gn= is =C-M-n=.
- =SPC= switches literal mode on and off: following keys have no modifier. =c SPC g= is =C-c g=, not =C-c C-g=.
- =c= first gives =C-c= and starts an Org chain: =c t= is =C-c C-t=, =c c= is =C-c C-c=. Punctuation stays as typed (=c .= is =C-c .=).
- Arrows, =Tab= and =Return= typed alone are never controlled, so moving around still works.

* Try it
Each exercise starts with god-mode on and the cursor on the heading named. Use the outline below.

| Press | Emacs chord | What happens |
|---+---+---|
| =↓= or =↑= | =<down>=, =<up>= | next or previous visible line (in a table, the next or previous row) |
| =Tab= | =Tab= | cycle the focused heading's fold state |
| =S-Tab= | =S-Tab= | cycle the whole document: overview, then everything shown |
| =c t= | =C-c C-t= | cycle TODO, NEXT, DONE, none |
| =c ,= | =C-c ,= | cycle priority: none, A, B, C |
| =g↑= or =g↓= | =M-↑=, =M-↓= | move the heading up or down among its siblings |
| =g←= or =g→= | =M-←=, =M-→= | promote or demote the heading with its subtree |
| =g RET= | =M-RET= | new heading after this one, at the same level |
| =c n= and =c p= | =C-c C-n=, =C-c C-p= | next and previous heading, any level |
| =c f= and =c b= | =C-c C-f=, =C-c C-b= | next and previous heading at the same level |
| =c u= | =C-c C-u= | the parent heading |
| =c s= or =c d= | =C-c C-s=, =C-c C-d= | open the details editor to set SCHEDULED or DEADLINE |
| =c w= | =C-c C-w= | refile the heading |
| =c x i= and =c x o= | =C-c C-x C-i=, =C-c C-x C-o= | clock in and out |
| =c x j= | =C-c C-x C-j= | jump to the clocked-in heading |
| =c SPC a a=, =c SPC a t=, =c SPC a m=, =c SPC a s= | =C-c a a=, =C-c a t=, =C-c a m=, =C-c a s= | Agenda, TODO list, tag match, keyword search |
| =x s= | =C-x C-s= | save |
| =x SPC n s= and =x SPC n w= | =C-x n s=, =C-x n w= | narrow to the heading, and widen |
| =s= and =r= | =C-s=, =C-r= | search; on the Agenda, next and previous match |
| =/= | =C-/= | undo |
| =f= then =/= | =C-f= then =C-/= | redo (=f= arms the next =/=) |
| =g x= | =M-x= | the command palette |
| =h SPC m= | =C-h m= | Help, without leaving god-mode |

** i, a and e
These three are not chords; they are modeled loosely on vim. =i= edits the current line with the cursor at its start. Press =a= first and it starts at the start of the line, or =e= and it starts at the end. They act only as the first key of a sequence: =g i= is still =M-i=.

* An outline to practice on
** TODO Write the report
SCHEDULED: <2026-11-02 Mon>
*** NEXT Outline the sections
*** Collect the figures
** TODO Plan the trip
*** Book the flights
*** Reserve a hotel
** Budget
| Item    | Cost |
|---------+------|
| Flights |  420 |
| Hotel   |  310 |

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- God-mode here is not the Emacs package itself, but its translation rules are followed, plus the =c= rule above, which is this app's own.
- =i=, =a=, =e= and =f= are this app's own keys. =f= stands in for the =C-f= god-mode users press to redo, since Emacs has no redo command.
- Some valid sequences say that they do nothing yet, rather than failing silently: =c c= (toggling a checkbox or running a block needs finer focus than a heading), =c |= and the table row and column inserts (use the +row and +col controls under a table), and =c l= and =c o=.
- Opening Capture or a picker (=c SPC c=, or =c t= on a heading with no state and several workflows) leaves god-mode and shows tappable buttons, each with a one-letter hotkey you can type.

#+TITLE: Habits
#+STARTUP: showall

A habit is an open TODO with =:STYLE: habit= and a repeating =SCHEDULED:= date. In the Agenda, its row gets a strip of days: 21 before today, today and 7 after. This file holds four habits. Open it as an Agenda File and compare the strips with the ones under each habit, drawn for Tuesday 13 October 2026. The strips are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) drew with =org-habit-build-graph=, and a test in this project checks that the app draws the same.

Each strip has two lines, one character for each day, the first being 22 September. The first line marks the days: =*= is a day the habit was done, =!= is today. The second line gives the color: =b= blue (not due yet), =g= green (can be done), =y= yellow (last chance) and =r= red (overdue). The third line is the shade: =p= plain, =l= the lighter shade Emacs uses for a day that is not done, not today and not a past overdue day. A habit is done when its =:LOGBOOK:= has a =State "DONE"= line for the day.

* TODO Shave
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-13 Tue .+2d/4d>
:PROPERTIES:
:STYLE: habit
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 20:14]
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-08 Thu 08:00]
:END:

** Every two days, no later than every four
=.+2d/4d= means every 2 days, and no later than every 4. The habit was done on 8 and 11 October. After each, it turns green when it can be done again and yellow on the last day to do it.

#+NAME: shave
#+begin_example
................*..*.!......
bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbgbggbggyrrrr
llllllllllllllllpllplpllllll
#+end_example

* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-04 Sun .+3d/5d>
:PROPERTIES:
:STYLE: habit
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-01 Thu 09:00]
:END:

** Overdue
The plants were last watered on 1 October and are watered every 3 to 5 days. The strip turns red after the last day.

#+NAME: water
