#+TITLE: Holidays
#+STARTUP: content

The holidays the Agenda, the diary and *List holidays…* show are Emacs's =calendar-holidays=, put together from groups. This file shows which are on, how to turn every one on, how to switch some off, and how to add your own; the results are what Emacs 29.3 listed for 2026 (time zone America/New_York), and a test checks the app lists the same.

* How to try an example
Copy the Lisp into Settings → Advanced → *Lisp init*, then open the palette and run *List holidays…* with 2026 as both years. The same text works in an Emacs init file: put it where it runs before the calendar loads, because Emacs builds =calendar-holidays= from the group variables once, when it loads. (Setting =calendar-holidays= itself works at any time.)

Holidays reach the Agenda through the diary: with =org-agenda-include-diary= on they are the "Diary:" rows. =diary-show-holidays-flag= set to =nil= leaves them out.

* What is on, and what is not
Seven groups come with Emacs, and two more are yours. All are on, except the extra entries each of five groups holds back behind a flag:

| Variable                      | Holds                                              | Flag for the extra entries                  |
|-------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------|
| =holiday-general-holidays=    | United States public days and observances          |                                             |
| =holiday-christian-holidays=  | Ash Wednesday, Good Friday, Easter, Christmas      | =calendar-christian-all-holidays-flag=      |
| =holiday-hebrew-holidays=     | the festivals and Hanukkah                         | =calendar-hebrew-all-holidays-flag=         |
| =holiday-islamic-holidays=    | Islamic New Year, the start of Ramadan             | =calendar-islamic-all-holidays-flag=        |
| =holiday-bahai-holidays=      | the Bahá’í festivals and three days of Ridvan      | =calendar-bahai-all-holidays-flag=          |
| =holiday-oriental-holidays=   | Chinese New Year                                   | =calendar-chinese-all-holidays-flag=        |
| =holiday-solar-holidays=      | equinoxes, solstices, daylight saving time changes |                                             |
| =holiday-local-holidays=      | yours, for where you live (empty)                  |                                             |
| =holiday-other-holidays=      | yours, any others (empty)                          |                                             |

Every flag is =nil= until you set it. The general group is American; "Replace a group" below changes it.

** What is on by default
With no Lisp init at all, Emacs lists these (2026, time zone America/New_York). Every ~calendar-*-all-holidays-flag~ is off.

** Remove several entries
~remove~ calls nest. An entry is matched as written, quotes and spaces aside, so copy it from the group (the lists are in [[https://git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/emacs.git/tree/lisp/calendar/holidays.el][holidays.el]]).

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq holiday-general-holidays
      (remove '(holiday-fixed 2 2 "Groundhog Day")
              (remove '(holiday-fixed 4 1 "April Fools' Day")
                      (remove '(holiday-float 10 1 2 "Columbus Day")
                              holiday-general-holidays))))
#+end_src

** Name the list yourself
~calendar-holidays~ is what Emacs uses; the groups are only how it is first put together. Setting it directly (after ~(require 'holidays)~, so the group variables exist) picks the groups you want. Here, the Christian and Islamic groups and nothing else:

(setq calendar-holidays
      (append holiday-christian-holidays
              holiday-islamic-holidays))

* Add your own
The forms Emacs gives you, each in ~holiday-local-holidays~ (or ~holiday-other-holidays~). The manual describes them in [[https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/emacs/Holidays.html][Holidays]] and [[https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/emacs/Advanced-Calendar_002fDiary-Usage.html][Advanced Calendar/Diary Usage]]; the source is [[https://git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/emacs.git/tree/lisp/calendar/holidays.el][holidays.el]].

** Add a fixed date: holiday-fixed
~(holiday-fixed MONTH DAY "NAME")~: the same date every year.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq holiday-local-holidays
      '((holiday-fixed 3 14 "Pi Day")
        (holiday-fixed 6 19 "Juneteenth")))
#+end_src

Compared with the default list for 2026 (~+~ is added, ~-~ is gone):

#+begin_example
+ Saturday, March 14, 2026: Pi Day
+ Friday, June 19, 2026: Juneteenth
#+end_example

** Add "the Nth weekday": holiday-float
~(holiday-float MONTH DAYNAME N "NAME" [DAY])~. DAYNAME is 0 for Sunday to 6 for Saturday; N counts from the start of the month, or from its end when negative. A DAY makes it the Nth weekday on or after that day: the Tuesday after the first Monday of November is the first Tuesday on or after November 2.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq holiday-local-holidays
      '((holiday-float 11 2 1 "Election Day" 2)
        (holiday-float 4 5 -1 "Arbor Day")))
#+end_src

Compared with the default list for 2026 (~+~ is added, ~-~ is gone):

#+begin_example
+ Friday, April 24, 2026: Arbor Day
+ Tuesday, November 3, 2026: Election Day
#+end_example

~(holiday-easter-etc DAYS "NAME")~: days after Easter, or before it when negative.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq holiday-local-holidays
      '((holiday-easter-etc 1 "Easter Monday")
        (holiday-easter-etc 7 "Low Sunday")))
#+end_src

Compared with the default list for 2026 (~+~ is added, ~-~ is gone):

#+end_example

#+TITLE: Calendar export
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for iCalendar export. The palette's *Export → iCalendar* (in Emacs, =org-icalendar-export-to-ics=) turns timestamps into events. =icalendar.ics= beside this file is what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) wrote for it with the time zone America/New_York, and the app writes the same text, apart from =DTSTAMP= (the time of export). The last section says where the two differ.

* Meetings
** Planning meeting
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: planning-1
:LOCATION: Room 4
:END:
<2026-11-03 Tue 10:00-11:30> Agree the quarter's goals.

** Team lunch
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: lunch-1
:END:
<2026-11-05 Thu 12:00>

* Dates without a time
** Dentist
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: dentist-1
:END:
<2026-11-10 Tue>

** Conference
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: conf-1
:END:
<2026-11-16 Mon>--<2026-11-18 Wed>

* Repeating
** Pay rent
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: rent-1
:END:
<2026-11-01 Sun +1m>

* Tasks with a deadline or a schedule
** TODO File the report                                             :work:
DEADLINE: <2026-11-20 Fri> SCHEDULED: <2026-11-18 Wed>
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: report-1
:END:

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- A heading with no =:ID:= gets a random =UID= from Emacs and a stable one from the app (made from the file name and the heading), so the same event keeps its identity when you export again. The headings above carry an =:ID:= so the files can be compared.
- The =TODO= heading at the end is left out by both, because =org-icalendar-include-todo= is =nil= in Emacs and in the app; set it in Settings → Export to have tasks written.
- The =PRODID= names the login name of the user who exported.

* Importing
=icalendar-import.ics= beside this file is a small calendar from another app; *Import → iCalendar* (in Emacs, =icalendar-import-file=) turns it into headings:
- /Design review/ keeps its organizer, attendees and attachment, and its 15-minute reminder becomes =:APPT_WARNTIME: 15=.
- /Gym/ (Monday and Thursday, six times, one day skipped) cannot be a repeater, so it becomes a =<%%(...)>= expression with the skipped day left out and the time first in the title. =COUNT= is turned into an end date; Emacs's own import gets this count wrong.
- /Clinic day/ (the second Tuesday, until March) uses =diary-float=.
- /Pay rent/ is a plain monthly repeater, =+1m=.

#+TITLE: Inline LaTeX
#+STARTUP: showall

Math written between LaTeX delimiters is typeset where you read it: in the outline, in Docs and in HTML export. The file's text is not changed, and editing a line shows the source. LaTeX export writes the math as it is, and ODT export turns each fragment into an embedded formula.

* The delimiters
| Write | Kind | Notes |
|---+---+---|
| =\(...\)= | inline | Org's recommended form; no restrictions |
| =\[...\]= | display | may span lines |
| =$$...$$= | display | may span lines |
| =$...$= | inline | one character is enough (=$x$=); no space just inside the dollar signs |
| =\begin{env}...\end{env}= | display | =\begin= starts a line |

* Inline
The quadratic formula is \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

Euler's identity, $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$, ties five constants together. A sum such as \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) stays on the line it is written in.

Greek letters and symbols: \(\alpha + \beta \le \gamma\), \(A \cup B \subseteq C\), \(\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\infty\).

* Money stays money
A dollar sign next to a number is not math: it costs $5 and $10 total. This is Org's own rule: the opening =$= cannot be followed by a space, comma, period or semicolon, and the closing =$= must be followed by a space, the end of the line or punctuation. So =$a$b= and =$x$-y= stay text.

* Display
\[
\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}
\]

$$
\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}
$$

** Several equations lined up
\begin{align}
E &= mc^2 \\
F &= ma \\
a^2 + b^2 &= c^2
\end{align}
The three equations line up at the =&= marks and are numbered (1) to (3), as KaTeX does for =align=. The =\\= here ends an equation; it is not Org's hard line break.

** A matrix
\begin{equation}
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}

* In headings, lists and tables
** The slope \(m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\) in a heading
- A list item with \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\)
- Another with $\pi r^2$

| Shape  | Area                |
|--------+---------------------|
| Circle | \(\pi r^2\)         |
| Square | \(s^2\)             |

* When a fragment will not render
KaTeX covers a large part of LaTeX, not all of it. A fragment it cannot read shows its source in a dashed box: \(\notacommand{x}\). KaTeX does not treat =%= as a comment.

* Where the app differs from Emacs
Emacs draws fragments as images made by LaTeX when you toggle previews. Here KaTeX draws them as you read, so spacing can differ slightly.

#+TITLE: Lisp init
#+STARTUP: showall

Settings → Advanced → *Lisp init* takes Emacs Lisp, run as Emacs runs an init file. Each section below shows the Lisp to type and, under it, what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) gives for the expressions listed after it; the app gives the same. A form that fails does not stop the ones after it.

* Settings
=setq= gives a setting a value, written as in Emacs. Numbers can be computed.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-agenda-files '("github:home.org" "github:journal.org")
      org-deadline-warning-days (* 2 7)
      org-log-done 'time)
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
org-agenda-files
  => ("github:home.org" "github:journal.org")
org-deadline-warning-days
  => 14
org-log-done
  => time
#+end_example

* Lists
=add-to-list= and =push= add to a list you have set. A third argument of =t= adds at the end.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq my-list nil my-other nil)
(add-to-list 'my-list 'a)
(add-to-list 'my-list 'b t)
(add-to-list 'my-list 'a)
(push "z" my-other)
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
my-list
  => (a b)
my-other
  => ("z")
#+end_example

* A variable that was never set
=add-to-list= and =push= need a variable that has a value. On one that was never set, Emacs reports that it is void, and the form after it still runs. The variables the app knows, such as =org-modules= and =org-capture-templates=, always have one.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(add-to-list 'never-set 'a)
(push 1 never-set-either)
(add-to-list 'org-modules 'org-habit)
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
(boundp 'never-set)
  => nil
(car org-modules)
  => org-habit
#+end_example

Messages:
#+begin_example
Symbol's value as variable is void: never-set
Symbol's value as variable is void: never-set-either
#+end_example

* Functions and computed values
All of Lisp is there to compute a value: =defun=, =let=, loops, =format=. What the init defines is there for diary entries and holiday lists too.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(defun double (n) (* 2 n))
(setq doubled (let ((acc nil))
                (dolist (x '(1 2 3)) (push (double x) acc))
                (nreverse acc)))
(setq label (mapconcat #'identity '("x" "y") "-"))
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
doubled
  => (2 4 6)
label
  => "x-y"
(format "%s has %d items, %.1f%%" label (length doubled) 12.5)
  => "x-y has 3 items, 12.5%"
#+end_example

* Holidays
The holiday lists are variables. This switches the general holidays off and adds a day of your own. See =holidays.org= for every entry and flag.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq holiday-general-holidays nil)
(setq holiday-other-holidays
      '((holiday-fixed 3 14 "Pi Day")
        (holiday-float 11 4 4 "Thanksgiving")))
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
holiday-general-holidays
  => nil
holiday-other-holidays
  => ((holiday-fixed 3 14 "Pi Day") (holiday-float 11 4 4 "Thanksgiving"))
#+end_example

* A capture template
Templates are read as Emacs reads them and are what the Capture list shows. See =capture-templates.org=.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-capture-templates
      '(("t" "Todo" entry (file+headline "gtd.org" "Tasks")
         "* TODO %?\n  %i")))
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
org-capture-templates
  => (("t" "Todo" entry (file+headline "gtd.org" "Tasks") "* TODO %?
  %i"))
(car (car org-capture-templates))
  => "t"
#+end_example

* LaTeX settings
The LaTeX export reads the ox-latex variables, among them the source block backend and the table options.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-latex-src-block-backend 'minted
      org-latex-tables-booktabs t
      org-latex-default-figure-position "htbp")
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
org-latex-src-block-backend
  => minted
org-latex-tables-booktabs
  => t
org-latex-default-figure-position
  => "htbp"
#+end_example

* A function as a setting
Some settings name a function. =org-latex-format-headline-function= formats every section title; the Agenda settings such as =org-agenda-cmp-user-defined= work the same way. The expressions below call the function directly.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-latex-format-headline-function
      (lambda (todo todo-type priority text tags info)
        (concat (if todo (format "[%s] " todo) "") (upcase text))))
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
(funcall org-latex-format-headline-function "TODO" (quote todo) nil "Write" nil nil)
  => "[TODO] WRITE"
(funcall org-latex-format-headline-function nil nil nil "Plan" nil nil)
  => "PLAN"
#+end_example

* Capture templates
=add-to-list= adds a template to =org-capture-templates=, which the Capture list shows. The same forms work in a file read with =(load "github:init.el")=.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq org-capture-templates nil)
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("w" "Web page or text" entry (file+headline "inbox.org" "Inbox") "* %a"))
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("j" "Journal" entry (file+olp+datetree "journal.org") "* %?"))
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
(mapcar (function car) org-capture-templates)
  => ("j" "w")
(nth 1 (car org-capture-templates))
  => "Journal"
#+end_example

* When a form fails
A form that fails shows Emacs's message in the status line, and the forms after it still run.

#+begin_src emacs-lisp
(setq before 1)
(car 5)
(no-such-function 1)
(setq after 2)
#+end_src

Values:
#+begin_example
before
  => 1
after
  => 2
#+end_example

Messages:
#+begin_example
Wrong type argument: listp, 5
Symbol's function definition is void: no-such-function
#+end_example

* Reading more from a file
=(load "github:file.el")= reads another file as part of the init, and the Agenda's *Refresh* reads it again. Emacs loads a file of your disk instead. Capture templates set in that file are in the Capture list too.

* Where the app differs from Emacs
The init runs on the app's own interpreter, which has the common functions and the Org read-only functions, not all of Emacs. A function it lacks fails with Emacs's message for a void function. A program that never ends stops with a message.

App only: =(load "github:file.el")= and the settings the app adds (`org-xx-…`).

#+TITLE: Logging
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for the notes and log items that go with a change of TODO state. What a plain change writes is in =todo-states.org=; this file adds the keyword settings with =@=, =!= and =/=, notes, and the =LOGGING= and =LOG_INTO_DRAWER= properties. Each section shows a heading before, and after the state in the title is set, with the note typed when one is asked for; the clock reads 2026-10-11 16:30. The "after" texts are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) left. Lines that start with =*= or =#+= carry a comma, as org requires inside a block.

A keyword's setting is written in the =#+TODO:= line in parentheses: its fast key, then =@= (ask for a note) or =!= (write a time stamp) for entering the state, and after a =/= the same for leaving it.

* A note when a state is entered
An =@= on a keyword asks for a note each time the heading enters it. The item and the note go together.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@) | DONE(d!)
,* TODO Call the bank
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
The number is on the card.
#+END_SRC

After setting NEXT and typing the note "Waiting for the card":
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@) | DONE(d!)
,* NEXT Call the bank
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30] \\
  Waiting for the card
The number is on the card.
#+END_SRC

* A note of several lines
Every line after the first is indented under the item.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@) | DONE(d!)
,* TODO Call the bank
#+END_SRC

After setting NEXT and typing the note "Waiting for the card. / Pat said Tuesday.":
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@) | DONE(d!)
,* NEXT Call the bank
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30] \\
  Waiting for the card.
  Pat said Tuesday.
#+END_SRC

* A note left empty
Leaving the note empty keeps the item without text.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@) | DONE(d!)
,* TODO Call the bank
#+END_SRC

After setting NEXT and leaving the note empty:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@) | DONE(d!)
,* NEXT Call the bank
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* A time stamp when a state is left
=NEXT(n/!)= does not log on the way in, but logs a time stamp on the way out, whatever the next state's own setting.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n/!) | DONE(d)
,* NEXT Call the bank
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n/!) | DONE(d)
,* DONE Call the bank
- State "DONE"       from "NEXT"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* Entering with a note, leaving with a time stamp
=NEXT(n@/!)= asks for a note on the way in; on the way out it writes only the item.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@/!) | DONE(d)
,* NEXT Call the bank
#+END_SRC

After setting TODO:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n@/!) | DONE(d)
,* TODO Call the bank
- State "TODO"       from "NEXT"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* A note when a task is closed
=#+STARTUP: lognotedone= asks for a note on the way to a done state and writes =CLOSED:=. The note item is "CLOSING NOTE".

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: lognotedone
,* TODO Send the form
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE and typing the note "Mailed it with the receipt.":
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: lognotedone
,* DONE Send the form
CLOSED: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30] SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
- CLOSING NOTE [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30] \\
  Mailed it with the receipt.
#+END_SRC

* A note for a repeating task
=#+STARTUP: lognoterepeat= asks for a note each time a repeating task is marked done.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: lognoterepeat
,* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon +1w>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE and typing the note "Gave the ferns extra.":
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: lognoterepeat
,* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon +1w>
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30] \\
  Gave the ferns extra.
#+END_SRC

* One subtree logs; the rest does not
The =LOGGING= property takes the same words as =#+STARTUP:= and is inherited, so everything below this heading gets =CLOSED:= when it is done.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes
:PROPERTIES:
:LOGGING: logdone
:END:
,** TODO File the form
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE on =File the form=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* Taxes
:PROPERTIES:
:LOGGING: logdone
:END:
,** DONE File the form
CLOSED: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* One subtree logs into a drawer
=LOG_INTO_DRAWER: t= puts the log items of this subtree in =:LOGBOOK:=.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n!) | DONE(d!)
,* Taxes
:PROPERTIES:
:LOG_INTO_DRAWER: t
:END:
,** TODO File the form
,* TODO Call Pat
#+END_SRC

After setting NEXT on =File the form=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n!) | DONE(d!)
,* Taxes
:PROPERTIES:
:LOG_INTO_DRAWER: t
:END:
,** NEXT File the form
:LOGBOOK:
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:

,* TODO Call Pat
#+END_SRC

* Logging switched off for a subtree
=LOGGING: nil= turns off =CLOSED:= and repeat logging for the subtree, even when the file asks for them.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone
,* Taxes
:PROPERTIES:
:LOGGING: nil
:END:
,** TODO File the form
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE on =File the form=:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone
,* Taxes
:PROPERTIES:
:LOGGING: nil
:END:
,** DONE File the form
#+END_SRC

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- When the app starts a =:LOGBOOK:= on the last heading of a file, and nothing follows the heading, it leaves no blank line after =:END:=; Emacs leaves one.

#+TITLE: Plots

A =#+PLOT:= line directly above a table graphs it. In the app, *📊 Plot* below the table shows the graph inline; tap again to hide it. The app reads org-plot's own options, so a line copied from Emacs works. Under each table is what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) hands to gnuplot, and the app draws the same series. The drawing itself is the app's own; Emacs needs gnuplot to draw.

* Lines
A =#+PLOT:= line directly above a table graphs it. =ind= is the column for the x position and =deps= the columns to draw, each as its own line, named by the header row. Tap *📊 Plot* below the table to see the graph.

* Keyword search
=org-search-view= (*Search → Keyword search*) takes words, ="phrases"=, =+word= and =-word=, and a regular expression in braces. A word looks at the heading, its tags, properties and text, but not at its sub-headings. A string that starts with a word is one phrase; one that starts with =+= or =-= is a list of words that must (or must not) be there. A leading =*= limits it to headings, =!= to TODO headings, and =:= to whole words.

- =wifi= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Buy a colour printer
- =+wifi -ethernet= :: Fix the wifi router
- =+wifi +ethernet= :: Buy a computer; Buy a colour printer
- =+"colour chart"= :: Fix the wifi router
- =colour chart= :: Fix the wifi router
- =+budget -{Q4}= :: Buy a computer
- =*+fix= :: Fix the wifi router; Fix the budget
- =!fix= :: Fix the wifi router; Fix the budget
- =:+color +colors= :: (none)
- ={wi.?fi}= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Buy a colour printer

* Regular expressions
In regex mode a pattern is in Emacs's syntax and is matched against each entry (its heading line, planning, drawers and text, as =string-match= would see it): =\(= =\)= group, =\|= chooses, =\{n,m\}= repeats, and a bare =(=, =)=, ={= or =}= is itself. Case is ignored.

- =^\*+ \(TODO\|DONE\)= :: Buy a computer; Buy a colour printer; Fix the budget
- =^colou?r= :: Colour palette for slides
- =\(Buy\|Fix\)= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Buy a colour printer; Fix the budget
- =\<ca= :: Fix the wifi router
- =\(a\)\1= :: Notes (a)
- =[[:digit:]]+= :: Buy a computer; Fix the budget; Notes (a)
- =(draft)= :: Notes (a)
- ={final}= :: Notes (a)
- =a\{2\}= :: Notes (a)
- =a\{3,\}= :: (none)
- =\bwi= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Buy a colour printer
- =ETHERNET= :: Buy a computer; Buy a colour printer
- =\_<port\_>= :: Buy a computer

* Filters
A query of =tag:=, =todo:=, =priority:= and =key:value= filters stands for a Match query (the text after "as"), and finds the same headings. Tags are inherited, properties are not. A =key:value= matches when the value contains the text.

- =tag:urgent= as =urgent= :: Fix the wifi router; Fix the budget
- =-tag:work= as =-work= :: Fix the wifi router; Buy a colour printer; Notes (a)
- =tag:work todo:TODO= as =work/TODO= :: Buy a computer; Fix the budget
- =todo:WAITING= as =/WAITING= :: Fix the wifi router
- =todo:TODO|WAITING= as =/TODO|WAITING= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Fix the budget
- =-todo:DONE= as =/-DONE= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Plan the quarter; Fix the budget; Colour palette for slides; Notes (a)
- =priority:A= as =PRIORITY="A"= :: Buy a computer
- =assignee:Bob= as =assignee={Bob}= :: Buy a computer; Fix the budget
- =assignee:Bob|Alice= as =assignee={Bob\|Alice}= :: Buy a computer; Fix the wifi router; Fix the budget
- =-assignee:Bob= as =assignee<>"Bob"= :: Fix the wifi router; Buy a colour printer; Plan the quarter; Colour palette for slides; Notes (a)

* Replace
*Replace* in the options popover starts a query-replace of the search text. In the lines below, a minus is the line before and a plus the line after replacing every match; the other lines of the outline stay as they are. A regexp replacement refers to a group as =\1= in Emacs.

Replace the text =wifi= with =Wi-Fi=:

#+TITLE: Table formulas
#+STARTUP: showall
#+CONSTANTS: tax=0.08 g=9.81

A cookbook for =#+TBLFM:= formulas. Each table holds its formula on the line below it. Use *🔢 Calc* under a table (or the command palette's *Recalculate all tables*; in Emacs, =C-c C-c= on the formula line or =C-u C-c *=). The results stored here are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) computes, and the app gives the same; the last section says where the two differ.

* Row and column totals
Column formulas (=$N=) skip the rows above the first rule. A cell formula (=@N$M=) writes one cell.

| Item   | Price | Qty | Total |
|--------+-------+-----+-------|
| Pens   |  1.50 |   4 |  6.00 |
| Books  | 12.00 |   2 | 24.00 |
| Paper  |  4.25 |   3 | 12.75 |
|--------+-------+-----+-------|
| Totals |       |   9 | 42.75 |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2*$3;%.2f::@5$3=vsum(@2..@4)::@5$4=vsum(@2..@4);%.2f

* Named columns and parameters
A row marked =!= names the columns, a row marked =$= holds parameters, and =#= marks the rows to calculate. =tax= below also comes from the =#+CONSTANTS:= line at the top; the table's own parameter wins.

| ! | Item              | Price | Qty |   Tot |
|---+-------------------+-------+-----+-------|
| $ | tax=0.1           |       |     |       |
| # | Pen               |  1.50 |   4 |  6.60 |
| # | Book              | 12.00 |   2 | 26.40 |
| / | note: not counted |       |     |       |
#+TBLFM: $5=$Price*$Qty*(1+$tax);%.2f

* Ranges between rules
=@I..@II= is the data between the first two rules. =@>= is the last row and =$>= the last column.

| Region | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 | Year |
|--------+----+----+----+----+------|
| North  | 12 | 15 | 11 | 18 |   56 |
| South  |  9 | 14 | 10 | 13 |   46 |
| West   | 20 | 18 | 22 | 25 |   85 |
|--------+----+----+----+----+------|
| All    | 41 | 47 | 43 | 56 |  187 |
#+TBLFM: $6=vsum($2..$5)::@>$2..@>$6=vsum(@I..@II)

* Statistics
| Test | Score |
|------+-------|
| A    |    72 |
| B    |    88 |
| C    |    95 |
| D    |    61 |
| E    |       |
|------+-------|
| Sum  |   316 |
| Mean | 79.00 |
| Min  |    61 |
| Max  |    95 |
| Mid  |    80 |
| N    |     4 |
| SD   | 15.38 |
#+TBLFM: @7$2=vsum(@2..@6)::@8$2=vmean(@2..@6);%.2f::@9$2=vmin(@2..@6)::@10$2=vmax(@2..@6)::@11$2=vmedian(@2..@6)::@12$2=vcount(@2..@6)::@13$2=vsdev(@2..@6);%.2f

The blank score in row E is left out of every aggregate, so the mean is over four scores.

* Number formats
|      Value |     Fixed | Scientific | Engineering |
|------------+-----------+------------+-------------|
| 123456.789 | 123456.79 |     1.23e5 |       123e3 |
| 3.14159265 |      3.14 |     3.14e0 |      3.14e0 |
#+TBLFM: $2=$1;f2::$3=$1;s3::$4=$1;e3

* Rounding and math functions
|    x | floor | ceil | round |  sqrt |     x^2 |    ln |
|------+-------+------+-------+-------+---------+-------|
|  2.5 |     2 |    3 |     3 | 1.581 |    6.25 | 0.916 |
| 7.25 |     7 |    8 |     7 | 2.693 | 52.5625 | 1.981 |
|   16 |    16 |   16 |    16 | 4.000 |     256 | 2.773 |
#+TBLFM: $2=floor($1)::$3=ceil($1)::$4=round($1)::$5=sqrt($1);%.3f::$6=$1^2::$7=ln($1);%.3f

* Conditions and grades
Comparisons give 1 or 0. Nested =if= is an else-if chain; here it gives grade points.

| Student | Exam | Lab | Points |
|---------+------+-----+--------|
| Ana     |   92 |  88 |      4 |
| Ben     |   81 |  60 |      3 |
| Cy      |   55 |  90 |      0 |
| Dee     |   74 |  71 |      2 |
#+TBLFM: $4=if($2 >= 90 && $3 >= 80, 4, if($2 >= 80, 3, if($2 >= 60 && $3 >= 60, 2, 0)))

* Dates
Subtracting two timestamps gives the days between them.

| Start            | End              | Days |
|------------------+------------------+------|
| [2026-01-05 Mon] | [2026-03-20 Fri] |   74 |
| [2026-02-10 Tue] | [2026-02-24 Tue] |   14 |
#+TBLFM: $3=$2-$1

* Durations
Flags =T=, =U= and =t= read =H:MM= cells as durations and show =H:MM:SS=, =H:MM= or decimal hours.

| Task 1 | Task 2 | Total (T) | Total (U) | Hours (t) |
|--------+--------+-----------+-----------+-----------|
|   2:12 |   1:47 |  03:59:00 |     03:59 |      3.98 |
|   0:45 |   3:30 |  04:15:00 |     04:15 |      4.25 |
#+TBLFM: $3=$1+$2;T::$4=$1+$2;U::$5=$1+$2;t

* Constants
=g= comes from the =#+CONSTANTS:= line at the top of this file.

| Mass kg | Weight N |
|---------+----------|
|       2 |    19.62 |
|      10 |    98.10 |
#+TBLFM: $2=$1*$g;%.2f

* Several formulas, in order
Formulas do not run in the order written. Org sorts them by their target, and runs column formulas row by row before field formulas, so a formula sees the results of the ones that sort before it. Here =$3= is written first but runs after =$2=.

| Base | Doubled | Plus ten |
|------+---------+----------|
|    3 |       6 |       16 |
|    8 |      16 |       26 |
#+TBLFM: $3=$2+10::$2=$1*2

* Named fields
A row marked =_= names the field below each of its cells; a row marked =^= names the field above. A name can then stand for that field on the right of a formula, or be the target on the left: =$tax== writes that one field.

|   | Price | Tax   | Total  |
| _ | price | tax   | total  |
| # | 100   | 20.00 | 120.00 |
#+TBLFM: $tax=$price*0.2;%.2f::$total=$price*1.2;%.2f

* A default format
A =$= row can hold =%== and a format. It is added to a formula that has flags such as =N= but no format of its own, so one line sets the decimals for the table. A formula with no flags at all does not get it.

| $ | %=%.2f |   |      |
| # |      1 | 3 | 0.33 |
| # |      2 | 7 | 0.29 |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2/$3;N

* Dates in Calc formulas
A date or time stamp in a formula is a number of days, so the difference of two dates is a number of days, and a date plus a number is a date.

| Start            | End              | Days | Due (+30)        |
|------------------+------------------+------+------------------|
| <2026-10-01 Thu> | <2026-10-15 Thu> |   14 | [2026-10-31 Sat] |
| <2026-11-02 Mon> | <2026-12-25 Fri> |   53 | [2026-12-02 Wed] |
#+TBLFM: $3=$2-$1::$4=$1+30

* Number literals
Calc reads =2#101= as binary, =16#ff= as base 16, =8#17= as octal and =1e3= as a power of ten. Each field in the last row is the field above it plus one.

|    a |     b |     c |     d |
|------+-------+-------+-------|
| 8#17 | 2#101 | 16#ff |   1e3 |
|   16 |     6 |   256 | 1001. |
#+TBLFM: @3$1=@2$1+1::@3$2=@2$2+1::@3$3=@2$3+1::@3$4=@2$4+1

* Writing two values side by side
In Calc a number written next to a variable or a parenthesis multiplies, so =2$1= is twice the first column and =3($1+1)= is three times one more than it.

| x | 2x | sum |
|---+----+-----|
| 5 | 10 |  18 |
| 7 | 14 |  24 |
#+TBLFM: $2=2$1;N::$3=3($1+1);N

* Complex numbers
| z1     | z2     | Product  |
|--------+--------+----------|
| (1, 2) | (3, 4) | (-5, 10) |
#+TBLFM: $3=$1*$2

* Solving equations
Letters are variables. =solve(equation, variable)= solves for one of them, taking the positive root where there are two; an inequality keeps its direction, and turns around when the divisor is negative. A root of a negative number is complex.

| Equation    | Solved for x    |
|-------------+-----------------|
| a*x+b=c     | x = (c - b) / a |
| x^2-5*x+6=0 | x = 3           |
| sqrt(x)=3   | x = 9           |
| 2^x=8       | x = 3.          |
| -2*x>6      | -3 > x          |
| x^2=-4      | x = (0, 2)      |
#+TBLFM: $2=solve($1,x)

=fsolve= writes the choice between roots as =s1=. A list of equations and a list of unknowns give a system.

| Equation | Both roots     |
|----------+----------------|
| x^2=a    | x = s1 sqrt(a) |
| x^2=4    | x = 2 s1       |
#+TBLFM: $2=fsolve($1,x)

| Equations      | Unknowns | Solution                               |
|----------------+----------+----------------------------------------|
| [x+y=3, x-y=1] | [x, y]   | [x = 2, y = 1]                         |
| [x+y=a, x-y=b] | [x, y]   | [x = a + (b - a) / 2, y = (a - b) / 2] |
#+TBLFM: $3=solve($1,$2)

* Simplify and expand
=simplify= applies Calc's rules for sums, products, powers, roots, logarithms and trig functions; =expand= multiplies out sums.

| Expression  | simplify        | expand        |
|-------------+-----------------+---------------|
| x+y+x       | y + 2 x         | x + y + x     |
| (x+1)^2     | (x + 1)^2       | x^2 + 2 x + 1 |
| (x+1)*(x-1) | (x + 1) (x - 1) | x^2 - 1       |
#+TBLFM: $2=simplify($1)::$3=expand($1)

* Derivatives
=deriv(expr, x)= differentiates with Calc's rules, and a third argument puts a value in for x. A function Calc has no rule for comes back as =f'(x)=.

| Expression  | deriv(x)           |
|-------------+--------------------|
| x^3+2*x     | 3 x^2 + 2          |
| x*exp(x)    | exp(x) + x exp(x)  |
| ln(x)/x     | x^-2 - ln(x) / x^2 |
| sqrt(x^2+1) | x / sqrt(x^2 + 1)  |
#+TBLFM: $2=deriv($1,x)

* Intervals and chained comparisons
An interval has a bracket or parenthesis at each end for closed or open. It adds, multiplies and takes powers as a whole, and =in(x, interval)= tests membership. =1 <= x < 7= is the test =x in [1 .. 7)=.

| Interval | Times 2   | Squared   | Contains 3? |
|----------+-----------+-----------+-------------|
| [1 .. 5] | [2 .. 10] | [1 .. 25] |           1 |
| (0 .. 4] | (0 .. 8]  | (0 .. 16] |           1 |
#+TBLFM: $2=$1*2::$3=$1^2::$4=in(3,$1)

| x | 1 <= x < 7 |
|---+------------|
| 3 |          1 |
| 7 |          0 |
#+TBLFM: $2=1 <= $1 < 7

* Bars in cells
=orgtbl-ascii-draw= draws a bar for a value between a minimum and a maximum.

| Item | Sales | Bar          |
|------+-------+--------------|
| Mon  |    12 | WWWWV        |
| Tue  |    30 | WWWWWWWWWWWW |
| Wed  |    24 | WWWWWWWWWl   |
#+TBLFM: $3='(orgtbl-ascii-draw $2 0 30 12)

* Text from if
Calc writes a text result as character codes, so ="P"= shows as =[80]=. Use numbers when the result should read well (the grades table above does).

| Score | Result |
|-------+--------|
|    95 | [80]   |
|    40 | [70]   |
#+TBLFM: $2=if($1>=50,"P","F")

* Number formats
=f=, =n=, =s= and =e= format a float with that many decimals or digits, in fixed, normal, scientific and engineering style. A result that is a whole number is left alone. A float shows 8 digits by default, a whole float keeps its dot, and very small or large floats switch to scientific. =%.Ne= and =%g= are C-style.

|      Value |        f2 |      n3 |      s3 |     e3 |     %.2e |   Default |
|------------+-----------+---------+---------+--------+----------+-----------|
| 123456.789 | 123456.79 | 123000. |  1.23e5 |  123e3 | 1.23e+05 | 123456.79 |
|   0.000314 |    3.1e-4 | 3.14e-4 | 3.14e-4 | 314e-6 | 3.14e-04 |   3.14e-4 |
|        2.5 |      2.50 |     2.5 |   2.5e0 |  2.5e0 | 2.50e+00 |       2.5 |
#+TBLFM: $2=$1;f2::$3=$1;n3::$4=$1;s3::$5=$1;e3::$6=$1;%.2e::$7=$1*1

* Division, remainder and fractions
=/= and =%= bind looser than =*=. =%= takes the sign of the divisor, =\= divides and rounds down, and a division by zero is left as written. =F= keeps fractions exact, written with a colon.

|  A | B |  A/B |   A%B |   A\B | A/B (F) |
|----+---+------+-------+-------+---------|
| 14 | 4 |  3.5 |     2 |     3 |     7:2 |
| -7 | 2 | -3.5 |     1 |    -4 |    -7:2 |
|  5 | 0 |  5/0 | 5 % 0 | 5 \ 0 |     5/0 |
#+TBLFM: $3=$1/$2::$4=$1%$2::$5=$1\$2::$6=$1/$2;F

* Dates and day numbers
A day number is counted from 1 January of year 1. =date= turns a date into that number and a number back into a date; adding to the bare date keeps it a date.

| Date             | Plus 30          | Day number | Back to date     |
|------------------+------------------+------------+------------------|
| [2026-01-15 Thu] | [2026-02-14 Sat] |     739631 | [2026-01-15 Thu] |
| [2026-03-31 Tue] | [2026-04-30 Thu] |     739706 | [2026-03-31 Tue] |
#+TBLFM: $2=$1+30::$3=date($1)::$4=date($3)

* Where Emacs and the app differ
Everything above gives the same result in both. These give a different result in Emacs 29.3:
- Digits above Calc's own accuracy: =sqrt(2);p50n50= ends in =...875377= in Emacs and =...8753769= in the app, which is the correct root.

App only: =uconv($1, "mi/hr", "m/s")= converts units (Emacs uses Calc's =u c= command); =#+PLOT:= draws inline (Emacs needs gnuplot and writes an image file); =date-to-time=, =format-time-string= and =now()= follow the device clock and the browser's date parser.

#+TITLE: Org Timer
#+STARTUP: showall

A timer for meetings, talks and practice. Open the command palette and choose:
- *Start timer* (=C-c C-x 0=, =org-timer-start=): a timer that counts up. It shows as =<0:12:03>= in the modeline.
- *Pause or continue timer* (=C-c C-x ,=), *Stop timer* (=C-c C-x _=).
- *Insert timer list item* (=C-c C-x -=, =org-timer-item=): adds =- 0:12:03 :: = to the end of the text of the heading you are on, and the next one goes under it. Write the note after the =::=.
- The *Timer* button of the text editors (=org-timer=) puts the time at the cursor.
- *Set countdown timer* (=C-c C-x ;=, =org-timer-set-timer=): minutes or =h:mm:ss=. On a heading with an =Effort=, it counts down that effort without asking. At zero, you get a reminder (and the sound of =org-clock-sound=).
- *Shift timer stamps in the text* (=org-timer-change-times-in-region=): moves every stamp in the heading's text by an amount such as =-0:08:26=; leave it empty to make the first one 0:00:00.

* Team meeting
The list below was made while the timer ran: start the timer with the meeting, then choose *Insert timer list item* at each topic.

- 0:00:12 :: Welcome and agenda
- 0:03:40 :: Release status: v701 is in testing
- 0:09:05 :: Open questions on the export options
- 0:14:30 :: Next steps

* The same notes, started late
The timer was started eight minutes into the meeting, so every stamp is 8:26 too small. *Shift timer stamps in the text* with =0:08:26= puts them right.

- 0:00:12 :: Welcome and agenda
- 0:03:40 :: Release status

* Focus block
:PROPERTIES:
:Effort: 0:25
:END:
*Set countdown timer* on this heading counts down 25 minutes, the effort, and says "Focus block: time out" at zero.

#+TITLE: Changing a TODO state
#+STARTUP: showall

A cookbook for what a change of TODO state writes. Each section shows a heading before, and after the state in the title is set; the clock reads 2026-10-11 16:30. The "after" texts are what Emacs 29.3 (Org 9.6.15) left, and the app gives the same. Lines that start with =*= or =#+= carry a comma, as org requires inside a block.

* A repeating task
Marking a repeating task done moves its date on, stamps =LAST_REPEAT=, logs the completion and puts the state back.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon +1w>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon +1w>
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* Repeater +1d
=+1d= adds one day to the old date, even if the result is still in the past.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Cumulate
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon +1d>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Cumulate
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-06 Tue +1d>
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* Repeater ++1d
=++1d= adds days until the date is in the future.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Catch up
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon ++1d>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Catch up
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon ++1d>
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* Repeater .+1d
=.+1d= counts from today.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Restart
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon .+1d>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Restart
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon .+1d>
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* Every repeating time stamp moves
A repeater in the title or text moves too, a time range keeps its end, and a =SCHEDULED= without a repeater is dropped.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Standup <2026-10-05 Mon 09:00-09:15 +1w>
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon>
DEADLINE: <2026-10-20 Tue +1m -3d>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,* TODO Standup <2026-10-12 Mon 09:00-09:15 +1w>
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
DEADLINE: <2026-11-20 Fri +1m -3d>
#+END_SRC

* Return to another state
=REPEAT_TO_STATE= names the state a repeating task goes back to, if the file has it.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT | DONE
,* TODO Review
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon +1d>
:PROPERTIES:
:REPEAT_TO_STATE: NEXT
:END:
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT | DONE
,* NEXT Review
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-06 Tue +1d>
:PROPERTIES:
:REPEAT_TO_STATE: NEXT
:LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* No repeat log
=#+STARTUP: nologrepeat= leaves out =LAST_REPEAT= and the log item.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: nologrepeat
,* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon +1w>
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: nologrepeat
,* TODO Water the plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon +1w>
#+END_SRC

* A closing time
=#+STARTUP: logdone= writes =CLOSED:= and nothing else.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone
,* TODO Write the report
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone
,* DONE Write the report
CLOSED: [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
#+END_SRC

* Reopening
Going back to an open state removes =CLOSED:=.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone
,* DONE Write the report
CLOSED: [2026-10-10 Sat 09:00]
#+END_SRC

After setting TODO:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone
,* TODO Write the report
#+END_SRC

* Logging every change
A =!= on a keyword logs each time the heading enters it. The item goes under the planning line, above the text.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n!) | DONE(d!)
,* NEXT Call the bank
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
The number is on the card.
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n!) | DONE(d!)
,* DONE Call the bank
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
- State "DONE"       from "NEXT"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
The number is on the card.
#+END_SRC

* Logging into the drawer
=#+STARTUP: logdrawer= puts log items in =:LOGBOOK:=.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone logdrawer
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n!) | DONE(d!)
,* TODO Call the bank
The number is on the card.
#+END_SRC

After setting NEXT:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+STARTUP: logdone logdrawer
,#+TODO: TODO NEXT(n!) | DONE(d!)
,* NEXT Call the bank
:LOGBOOK:
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:END:
The number is on the card.
#+END_SRC

* A log item above an existing drawer
Without =logdrawer=, a new item goes above a drawer the heading already has.

Before:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO | DONE(d!)
,* TODO Call the bank
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-10-10 Sat 09:00]--[2026-10-10 Sat 09:30] =>  0:30
:END:
#+END_SRC

After setting DONE:
#+BEGIN_SRC org
,#+TODO: TODO | DONE(d!)
,* DONE Call the bank
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-11 Sun 16:30]
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-10-10 Sat 09:00]--[2026-10-10 Sat 09:30] =>  0:30
:END:
#+END_SRC

* Where the app differs from Emacs
- =org-log-reschedule=, =org-log-redeadline= and =org-log-refile= are not applied.
- A note (=@=, =lognotedone=, =lognoterepeat=) is asked for in a panel after the state has changed; skipping it writes no item.

:PROPERTIES:

A mobile-first outliner for editing ~.org~ files in the browser. It works offline, needs no server and no account to use locally, and installs as a PWA.

This guide covers how to use it and, for anyone coming from Emacs, where it differs from real org-mode (see [[#differences-from-emacs-org-mode][Differences from Emacs org-mode]]).

** What org-pwa is (and isn't)
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: what-org-pwa-is-and-isnt
:END:

org-pwa is a *touch-first outline editor*, not a port of Emacs. It reads and writes real ~.org~ files and keeps anything it doesn't understand exactly as written. Editing is built around tapping and gestures rather than Emacs keybindings, and it implements a useful subset of org-mode, not all of it.

It is not org-mode with full parity: Babel runs JavaScript, and the rest is a subset (see [[#differences-from-emacs-org-mode][Differences from Emacs org-mode]]). It is for opening a real org file on your phone, reorganizing the outline, checking off tasks, editing tables and saving back to disk, GitHub or a WebDAV server.

-----

** Getting started
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: getting-started
:END:

1. Open the app and tap *File → Open* if no file is open.
2. The place bar at the top names where the list is looking; tap it to change place. It opens where you were last, in the folder you were last in for that place. The command palette's *Files (Dired)…* (~dired~) opens the same list in the folder of the current file.

   - *GitHub*: browse a repo set up in Settings and tap a file. *Type a path instead…* is always there for a path the listing doesn't show.
   - *WebDAV*: the same, for a WebDAV server set up in Settings.
   - *This device*: in Chrome or Edge on desktop, choose a folder once and its files are listed like the other places (the browser asks again for access in each new session). *Choose another file…* opens the system picker; Save writes straight back to the same file. In the Android app, the org-pwa folder is listed here.
   - *Import file* (instead of *This device* where File System Access is missing, such as iOS): reads a file once. Save downloads a new copy for you to put back (see [[#platform-support][Platform support]]).

   A place that is not set up says so and links to Settings; if the last place cannot be used, the list opens the most recent one that can and tells you. On a wide screen the places are listed beside the files.

3. Edit. Edits apply at once and are cached locally, so nothing is lost if you close the tab before saving.
4. Tap *Save* to write the file back to where it came from, or *Save As* to choose another destination.

*Menus and popups*: on a phone or tablet the menus and popups open as a bottom sheet. On a wide screen with a mouse the menus drop down under their button (*↑*, *↓*, *Home*, *End* and *Enter* move through them), and popups are centered dialogs. *Esc* closes either, and *Enter* accepts a question dialog such as a file path.

The modeline (see [[#modeline][Modeline and minibuffer]]) shows the filename, where it came from and whether it has unsaved edits. Once a second tab is open, the tab bar (see [[#tabs][Tabs]]) marks unsaved tabs with a dot.

-----

** Editing your outline
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editing-your-outline
:END:

- *Headings*: tap the title to show its actions: edit title, edit text, edit details (the general editor, below), add a sub-heading, TODO, move up and down, archive, attach (see [[#attachments][Attachments]]), delete, promote and demote. Most close the row after running; move and promote/demote stay open so you can repeat them. *Delete* always asks first, listing what would be lost, and every delete or discard confirmation in the app defaults to *Cancel*, so a stray Enter or tap never deletes. With a keyboard, the arrow keys move between the buttons and *Esc* closes the row.
- *TODO state*: tap the TODO badge to cycle the ~#+TODO:~ sequence (default ~TODO~, ~DONE~) one step at a time. The action menu's *TODO* button (~C-c C-t~) does the same, except that for a heading with no keyword in a file with more than one parallel ~#+TODO:~ workflow it opens a picker of every state of every workflow (see [[#progress-logging][Progress logging]]).
- *Fold and unfold*: tap the chevron to toggle a heading's subtree, or swipe left on a heading to cycle collapsed → children only → fully expanded.
- *Move*: drag the grip at the right of a heading to move it with its subtree (Settings → Editing and startup → Keyboard → *Drag handle on headings* moves it to the left or turns it off). The blue line snaps between two headings; moving sideways steps through the levels that fit, rightward being deeper, and a tag names the result (*into* a heading, *same level as* one, or *top level*). Letting go over the top bar or the mode line, or pressing Escape, cancels.
- *Complete or archive*: swipe right. A heading with an active TODO keyword jumps to the first DONE-type keyword. Otherwise it opens the Archive, Refile or Cancel prompt, and an archived heading unarchives directly.
- *Archive* (*Unarchive* for an archived heading) moves the subtree to its ~org-archive-location~ or back, from a panel that shows the destination first (see [[#archiving][Archiving]]). The ~:ARCHIVE:~ tag and ~ARCHIVE_*~ properties can be edited or removed in the general editor.
- *Moving in steps* (↑ ↓ ← →): ↑ and ↓ reorder a heading among its siblings with its subtree. ← promotes the heading with its subtree one level, as ~org-promote-subtree~ does: it stays where it is in the text, and the siblings after it become its children. → demotes it one level: after a sibling it becomes that sibling's last child, as a first child it stays under its parent. A top-level heading can't be promoted, and a short status message says so.
- *Heading alone*: ~org-promote~ and ~org-demote~ (~M-←~, ~M-→~, in the command palette) change the level of the heading only; its children keep theirs, so a demoted heading may stop being their parent. With ~org-adapt-indentation~ the lines under the heading follow. ~org-toggle-comment~ (~C-c ;~) puts ~COMMENT~ in front of the title or takes it off. ~org-insert-property-drawer~ adds an empty ~:PROPERTIES:~ drawer.
- *Sort*: ~org-sort-entries~ (~C-c ^~ on a heading, in the palette as ~org-sort~) asks for a key and sorts the heading's children, or the top-level entries when no heading is focused: ~a~ alphabetically, ~n~ numerically, ~t~ by the first timestamp, ~s~ by SCHEDULED, ~d~ by DEADLINE, ~c~ by the first inactive timestamp at the start of a line, ~p~ by priority, ~o~ by TODO order, ~r~ by a property, ~f~ by a function (one that gets the key, one that compares); a capital reverses. Case is ignored (*Sort entries, case sensitive* in the palette does not); keys are compared by character code.
- *The general editor* (📋 *Edit details*) is a popup with five tabs, so nothing is a long scroll: *Dates*, *Tags*, *Props*, *Files* and *More* (priority and tables). A tab you have edited shows a dot, and a note beside the buttons names them ("Changed: Dates, Tags"). Each tab shows how many items it holds.
  - *SCHEDULED, DEADLINE and a plain timestamp*: date and time pickers, a repeat selector (every N hours, days, weeks, months or years) and an optional warning delay (~-3d~ shows a deadline three days early). The three are independent, each with its own *Clear*. See [[#agenda][Agenda]] for how a plain timestamp differs (it doesn't carry forward, and lives in the title).
  - *Tags*: removable chips (tap to remove) and an input with an *Add* button (Enter also adds). Suggestions appear as you type: every tag used in the open document (from an agenda view, in your agenda files) plus tags declared on a ~#+TAGS:~ line or listed in ~org-tag-alist~ or ~org-tag-persistent-alist~, most used first, narrowed to what you typed and excluding tags the heading already has. One tap adds one.
  - *Priority*: a button for each priority of the range (A, B, C unless ~org-priority-highest~ and ~org-priority-lowest~ say otherwise) and None.
  - *Properties*: an editable key/value row for each, with a remove button and an *Add property* row. The Key field completes from every key used in the open document (from an agenda view, in your agenda files), most used first, plus ones the app reads or writes (~CUSTOM_ID~, ~EFFORT~, ~Effort_ALL~, ~ID~, the ~ARCHIVE_*~ set); other keys still work. A row with a blank key is dropped on commit. A property that is new or changed is written as Org writes it, with the ~:KEY:~ padded to ten columns (~:ID:       abc~). This is also how you set a ~CUSTOM_ID~ for ~[[#id]]~-style links (see [[#links-and-images][Links and images]]).

  Three buttons govern every tab: *Cancel* discards everything and closes, *Reset* restores every field to how it was when the editor opened, and *OK* commits every tab and closes. Nothing is written until *OK*. Above them are three immediate actions. *Add table* inserts a table into the body and closes the editor. *Delete table* removes the heading's most recently added table after a confirmation, and is disabled when there is none. *Attach* closes the editor and opens the attachment picker (see [[#attachments][Attachments]]). If any field has changed, these three first ask *Commit and continue*, *Discard and continue* or *Keep editing*; with no changes they act at once.

  Existing properties also show as a small read-only line under the heading while drawers are visible for it (~#+STARTUP: showeverything~, or manually cycled to fully expanded; see [[#folding-and-startup][Folding and #+STARTUP]]). Tapping it opens the action menu.

- *Text above the first heading*: the paragraphs, lists and tables before the first heading, and the file's ~#+KEY: value~ lines, show at the top of the Org view, whatever ~#+STARTUP~ says (as in Emacs, where that text is never folded). The text edits like any other, and the ~#+~ lines keep their place; the ~#+~ lines themselves are read-only here and are edited in View → Text. A file with no headings shows only this.
- *Block content* (~#+BEGIN_SRC~, ~#+BEGIN_QUOTE~, ~#+BEGIN_EXAMPLE~ and so on) is shown read-only, under the same drawer-visibility rule as properties. Folded, it shows a "collapsed block" label: tap it to reveal the content, and tap it again to re-fold. Edit blocks in [[#the-plain-text-editor][Text view]]. Any ~#+BEGIN_NAME~ and ~#+END_NAME~ pair works, and three names are displayed specially:
  - ~QUOTE~: inline markup is interpreted, and the block is indented on both margins with a left border.
  - ~VERSE~: inline markup is interpreted, and every source line stays its own line.
  - ~CENTER~: inline markup is interpreted, and its paragraphs are centered.

  Everything else (~SRC~, ~EXAMPLE~, ~COMMENT~, custom names) is shown literally.

  Export (see [[#export][Export]]) turns ~SRC~ into a code block with its language kept, ~QUOTE~ into a blockquote and drops ~COMMENT~. A ~SRC~ language is not syntax-highlighted in the outline, and only ~js~ blocks can run (see [[#source-blocks][Source blocks]]).

*** A heading's "text"
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: a-headings-text
:END:

Org has no separate description field: everything after a heading, up to the next heading, belongs to it, and can include several paragraphs, lists and tables in any order. *Edit text* opens all of it as one block of raw org syntax in a popup, like Settings' *Menu labels* editor (see [[#menu-customization][Menu customization]]): a large textarea with *Cancel* (discard and close), *Reset* (reload the original text and keep the popup open) and *OK* (save and close). The heading's rendered body is hidden from the outline while the popup is open. Typing ~- [ ]~ at the start of a line becomes a checklist item on save, as in the file.

** Undo/redo and History
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: undoredo-and-history
:END:

Every edit can be undone and redone: text, TODO state, priority, tags, properties, moving, archiving, capturing, all of it. The command palette's *Undo history* opens a panel with *‹ Undo* and *Redo ›* buttons, a list of every step since the file was opened (current position marked) and a *diff* toggle on each entry showing what it changed.

Undo and redo keep the folds you see: a heading stays open or closed as it was, matched by its title and its parents' titles; a heading the text change renamed or added opens as the file's ~#+STARTUP~ says.

The history is a tree. An edit made after an Undo starts a branch instead of discarding what was undone, and the panel shows the branches side by side, each indented from the step it follows. Tap any entry, on any branch, to jump there. Undo goes to the step before; Redo goes to the branch you were last on (the status line says ~branch 2 of 3~ when there is a choice). Dimmer entries are the ones Redo reaches, dimmest the other branches. The saved history keeps up to 200 steps, and branches you left go before the line you are working on.

A step is one completed edit action (saving a title, toggling a checkbox, archiving a heading), not a keystroke, and an edit that changes nothing adds none.

History is unlimited while a file stays open. It survives closing and reopening (the 200 most recent steps) only if the text on reopen matches what the app last had; if the file changed elsewhere, the old history is dropped. Undo and redo reapply the file's ~#+STARTUP~ visibility instead of keeping fold state.

Landing on a step identical to the last saved text clears the modified indicator.

*If the filename shows modified (red) and nothing you did explains it*, check the first history entry. If it reads "Opened (resumed unsaved local version)" instead of "Opened", the file had an unsaved edit from an earlier session, and reopening resumed it instead of starting from what is stored. Save to make that version the real one, or jump back in the history list if it wasn't what you wanted.

** Lists, tables, and body text
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: lists-tables-and-body-text
:END:

- *Lists*: ordered, unordered, checkboxes, description lists (~term :: description~) and nested sub-lists. Tap an item's text for edit, add-below and delete actions. *Add item below* puts the new item right under the item's line, as ~M-RET~ does, with the item's sub-items following it, and numbers an ordered list again (a description item gets an empty term only when the list's first item has one; an item with nothing after its bullet gets the new item above it; blank lines between items are kept). Lists inside drawers and example blocks edit like any other list. *Add checkbox below* does the same with a box. Deleting an item removes its text and sub-items.
- *Checkboxes* toggle between unchecked and done. A box that has boxes under it shows what they add up to (~[-]~ when some are done), as in Org, so tapping it changes nothing. A progress cookie (~[3/8]~, ~[40%]~, or the blank ~[/]~) in a heading's title or a list item is recalculated when a checkbox changes: a heading counts the top-level items of its own lists, an item counts its sub-list. ~:COOKIE_DATA: recursive~ counts nested items too. Changing a TODO state recalculates the parent heading's cookie from its TODO children (~:COOKIE_DATA: recursive~ reaches all descendants; ~checkbox~ keeps a heading on checkbox counting, ~todo~ on TODO counting). Percentages round down.
- *Tables*: tap a cell to edit it in place. The *⎌* button beside the field discards the edit and restores the cell's text (on a phone there is no Escape key). Row and column controls sit below the table; *⋯ Table* opens more (see [[#table-pad][Table pad]]). Every edit aligns the table the way ~org-table-align~ does (deleting a row leaves the others as they are), and the references in ~#+TBLFM:~ follow an inserted or deleted row or column. ~#+TBLFM:~ formulas are evaluated (see [[#table-formulas][Table formulas]]). *Header rows* are the rows before the table's first horizontal rule (~|---+---|~) and show bold; a table with no rule has no header, and a later rule only separates groups.
- *Paragraphs*: tap the text for edit, add-below and delete actions.
- *Captions, names and image sizes*: ~#+CAPTION:~, ~#+NAME:~, ~#+ATTR_HTML:~ (or ~#+ATTR_ORG:~), ~#+HEADER:~ and ~#+RESULTS:~ lines directly above a paragraph, image, table or block describe it. A caption shows in italics with its markup rendered; ~#+ATTR_HTML: :width 300 :align center~ sizes and centers the images in that paragraph (a plain number is pixels; ~%~ and ~em~ work). The other lines stay visible as small muted text, exactly as written.

Undo/redo covers every edit (see [[#undoredo-and-history][Undo/redo and History]]).

*** Table pad
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: table-pad
:END:

*⋯ Table*, below a table, opens a pad of buttons that act at the highlighted cell, the one you last tapped; the arrows at its top move it. Each button is an Org command, and holding one shows its key. They are in the command palette too (~org-table-insert-row~, ~org-table-kill-row~, ~org-table-sort-lines~ and the rest). In a table the M-arrow keys do these instead of moving headings. Sort offers a case-sensitive alphabetic pair (Emacs's ~C-u C-c ^ a~) after the eight kinds.

| Key | What it does |
|---+---|
| ~M-S-↓~, ~M-S-↑~ | Insert a row above the cursor; delete the row |
| ~M-↑~, ~M-↓~ | Move the row up or down (a rule counts as a row) |
| ~M-S-→~, ~M-S-←~ | Insert a column at the cursor; delete the column |
| ~M-←~, ~M-→~ | Move the column left or right |
| ~C-c -~ | Insert a rule below the row |
| ~C-c RET~ | Insert a rule and go to the row below it |
| ~C-c ^~ | Sort the rows between the nearest rules (the whole table if there are none) by the cursor's column |

*Sort* asks the way Emacs does: ~a~ alphabetic (ignoring case, by character code), ~n~ numeric (text that is not a number counts as 0), ~t~ time (timestamps and durations such as ~1:30~; other text counts as 0) or ~f~ function, and a capital letter reverses. ~f~ asks for the name of a function that gets the key from a field (a function that exists, such as ~length~ or one from your Lisp init), then for one that compares two keys; leave that empty for ~<~ on numbers and ~string<~ on strings. Rows that tie keep their order. The formulas follow a moved row or column; a sort leaves them alone.

With the cursor in the qty column of

#+begin_example
| fruit  | qty |
|--------+-----|
| apple  |   3 |
| banana |  12 |
| cherry |   7 |
#+end_example

~C-c ^ n~ puts the rows in the order apple, cherry, banana (3, 7, 12).

*** Table formulas
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: table-formulas
:END:

~#+TBLFM:~ formulas use Org's formula language with Calc's functions. *🔢 Calc* below a table recalculates it; *Recalculate all tables* in the command palette (~org-table-recalculate-buffer-tables~) does every table as one undo step. A malformed formula is reported and only its own table is skipped. Only the first ~#+TBLFM:~ line directly below a table counts. Worked examples, with the results Emacs gives, are in =examples/table-formulas.org=.

#+begin_example
| Item | Price | Qty |   Tot |
|------+-------+-----+-------|
| Pen  |  1.50 |   4 |  6.00 |
| Book | 12.00 |   2 | 24.00 |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2*$3;%.2f
#+end_example

| Name | What it does |
|---+---|
| ~+ - * / % \~ | Arithmetic as in Calc: ~/~, ~%~ and ~\~ bind looser than ~*~ (~14/4*2~ is ~14/8~), a minus looser than ~^~ (~-2^2~ is ~-4~). ~\~ divides and rounds down; whole numbers stay exact at any size; ~5/0~ is left as written |
| ~^~ | Exponent, right-associative (~2^3^2~ is 512) |
| ~sqrt(x)~ | Square root; a negative input gives a complex number |
| ~floor~, ~ceil~, ~round~, ~trunc~ | Round toward −∞, +∞, nearest (.5 goes away from zero) and zero; a second argument keeps decimals: ~round($1, 2)~ |
| ~sin~, ~cos~, ~tan~, ~arcsin~, ~arccos~, ~arctan~ | Degrees by default (flags ~D~ and ~R~); Calc's names, not ~asin~ |
| ~ln~, ~log10~, ~log(x, base)~, ~exp~, ~exp10~ | Logarithms (~log(x)~ is natural) and powers of e and 10 |
| ~pi~, ~inf~ | Constants written bare |
| ~2#101~, ~16#ff~, ~1e3~ | Numbers in a base from 2 to 36 and in scientific notation, in a field or a formula |
| ~$name~ | A constant from ~#+CONSTANTS:~, or a named column, parameter or field |
| ~vsum~, ~vmean~, ~vcount~, ~vmin~, ~vmax~, ~vmedian~ | Aggregates of a range; ~vcount~ counts non-blank cells |
| ~vvar~, ~vpvar~, ~vsdev~, ~vpsdev~ | Sample and population variance and standard deviation |
| ~if(c,t,f)~ | ~t~ if ~c~ is non-zero or non-empty, else ~f~; only that branch is evaluated |
| ~and~, ~or~, ~not~ | Function forms of the logical operators |
| ~string(ref)~, ~"text"~ | A cell's raw text, and a string literal (a string result shows as character codes, as in Calc). ~string("")~ gives an empty cell; ~string(x)~ shows a string, or a list of character codes, as text |
| ~typeof(x)~ | Calc's kind of value: 1 integer, 2 fraction, 3 float, 12 ~nan~ or ~inf~, 101 vector, 102 matrix |
| ~subvec(v, a, b)~, ~vlen(v)~ | The elements ~a~ to ~b-1~ of a vector or string, and how many elements it has |
| ~date(ref)~, ~date(Y,M,D)~, ~now()~, ~deg(x)~, ~date-to-time(ref)~ | Dates (below) |
| ~format-time-string(fmt, time, utc)~ | Emacs's, with every ~%~ code of [[#capture-templates][Capture templates]] |
| ~uconv(value, "from", "to")~ | Unit conversion (below) |

*Logic*: ~==~ (or ~=~), ~!=~, ~<~, ~>~, ~<=~, ~>=~ give 1 or 0 and bind tighter than ~&&~ and ~||~, which short-circuit like ~if~, so ~if($1 != 0, 100 / $1, 0)~ never divides by zero. ~!x~ is NOT. ~string($1) == "Sales"~ compares text; a bare ~$1 == "Sales"~ reads the cell as a number.

*Constants*: ~#+CONSTANTS: c=299792458 g=9.81~ defines ~$c~ and ~$g~. Several lines combine and a later value wins.

*Properties*: ~$PROP_name~ is the property ~name~ of the entry the table is in, inherited from its parents as ~org-entry-get~ does: ~$1=2*$PROP_rate~. A time such as ~08:00:00~ in it is read as a duration under ~T~.

*Other tables*: ~remote(name, @>$1)~ reads a field or range of the table with that ~#+NAME:~. The name can be a field of this table, ~remote($<, @>$1)~, and can be a number.

*Quoted references*: a reference inside quotes is pasted in as the field's text in parentheses, ~nan~ for an empty field under ~E~, and a range as ~[a,b,c]~: ~if("$1" == "nan", string(""), $1 + 1);E~ leaves an empty cell empty.

*Names in the table*: the first cell of a row marks it, as in Org.
- ~!~ names the columns below it: with ~| ! | Item | Price | Qty | Tot |~, ~$5=$Price*$Qty~ works (the marker column is column 1).
- ~$~ gives parameters as ~name=value~ cells, used as ~$name~. A parameter ~%=%.2f~ is added, as in Emacs, to a formula that has flags such as ~N~ but no format of its own.
- ~_~ and ~^~ name the field below or above each of its cells. ~$name~ reads that field, and ~$name=~ on the left sets it: ~$total=vsum(@2..@4)~.
- ~#~ and ~*~ rows are calculated when the table has any marked row, and then only those. Rows marked ~!~ ~$~ ~_~ ~^~ or ~/~ never are.

Names start with a letter and use letters, digits and ~_~. A column name wins over a parameter, and a parameter over a constant.

*Dates*: a cell with an Org timestamp is a date when referenced. Subtracting dates gives days (decimals if a time is present); adding a number shifts the date and keeps its day name: ~$1 + 14~ on ~<2026-08-25>~ gives ~[2026-09-08 Tue]~. ~date($1)~ is Calc's day number (~739631~ for ~[2026-01-15]~), ~date(739631)~ turns it back, and ~date(2026, 2, 29)~ rolls over to 1 March. ~($2 - $1) * 24;%.2f~ is hours between two timestamps. As in Calc, adding two dates adds their day numbers, and a date times a number stays symbolic. ~date-to-time~ also reads ISO 8601, RFC 822 and US dates. ~format-time-string("%Y-%m-%d", $1)~ gives ~2026-01-15~; ~time~ defaults to now and a non-zero ~utc~ formats in UTC.

*References*: ~$N~ is a column of the current row, ~@N$M~ a field, ~@-N~ and ~@+N~ rows relative to the target, ~@<~ ~@>~ ~$<~ ~$>~ the first and last row or column, and ~$1..$3~ or ~@1$1..@3$2~ a range (~@2..@6~ means those rows of the formula's own column). Rows count every row including the header. ~@I~, ~@II~ ... are horizontal rules (~@IIII~ is the fourth), ~@III+2~ is two rows after one, and ~vsum(@I..@II)~ covers the rows between two. The shorthand ~$M=~ skips the rows above the first rule that comes after a row.

*Targets and order*: a target is a field (~@N$M=~), a range (~@N$M..@N$M=~) or a column (~$M=~). Several formulas on one line are separated by ~::~ and run, as in Org, sorted by target: column formulas row by row, then field formulas.

*Blank and text cells*: a blank in a direct reference reads as 0 but is left out of a range. Text that is not a number leaves the formula as written (~label + 5~), as in Emacs; the ~N~ flag reads it as 0. A formula that fails writes ~#ERROR~ in that cell and the rest still updates; one that cannot be parsed is reported.

*Flags*: a trailing ~;flags~ string.

| Flag | Effect |
|---+---|
| ~%.Nf~, ~fN~ | Fixed, N decimals: ~$1/3;f2~ gives ~0.33~. Whole results are left alone |
| ~%.Ne~, ~%g~ | C-style: ~12345.678;%.2e~ gives ~1.23e+04~ |
| ~%d~ | Truncates toward zero |
| ~nN~, ~sN~, ~eN~ | Normal, scientific and engineering notation with N figures: ~3.14159265;n5~ gives ~3.1416~ |
| ~pN~ | Computes at N significant digits (arbitrary precision); add ~nN~ to show them: ~1/3;p20n20~ |
| ~E~, ~N~ | ~E~ keeps blanks as ~nan~; ~N~ reads non-numeric text (and with ~E~, blanks) as 0, and without ~E~ a result that is not a number is ~#ERROR~ |
| ~D~, ~R~ | Degrees (the default) or radians for trig |
| ~T~, ~U~, ~t~ | Durations: cells like ~HH:MM[:SS]~ are read as durations, and the result is ~HH:MM:SS~, ~HH:MM~ or decimal hours. ~org-table-duration-hour-zero-padding~ pads hours |
| ~F~ | Exact fractions, written with a colon as Calc does: ~1/3;F~ is ~1:3~ |

Text after the semicolon that is neither a flag nor a ~%~ format is written into the cell as it stands, as Emacs does.

*Units*: ~uconv($1, "mi/hr", "m/s")~ converts with the mathjs unit library, including compound units (~kg/m^3~). Temperatures convert as readings (~0 degC~ is ~32 degF~). An incompatible pair or unknown unit gives ~#ERROR~. Units follow Calc's names; ~tsp~ and ~tbsp~ also work. The full list is at https://mathjs.org/docs/datatypes/units.html.

*Complex numbers, vectors and algebra*:
- Complex: ~(re, im)~ or ~(r; θ)~, with ~i~ the number (0, 1): ~(1, 2) * (3, 4)~ is ~(-5, 10)~. ~re~, ~im~, ~conj~, ~abs~, ~arg~, ~polar~ and ~rect~ work.
- Vectors and matrices: ~[1, 2, 3]~ and ~[[1, 2], [3, 4]]~; ~+ -~ and ~* /~ by a number are elementwise, ~*~ is a dot or matrix product, and ~det~, ~inv~, ~trn~, ~tr~, ~cross~ and ~vlen~ work.
- Algebra: letters are variables and what cannot be reduced is written as Calc writes it (~x + x~ is ~2 x~). ~simplify~, ~esimplify~, ~expand~, ~deriv(sin(x)*x, x)~, ~prfac(360)~, and ~solve(a*x+b=c, x)~ for equations, inequalities and systems. ~fsolve~ writes ~s1~ and ~n1~ for the choices in a periodic solution. Intervals (~[1 .. 5]~) add, multiply and take powers.

*Raw Elisp*: a formula starting with a quote, ~'(orgtbl-ascii-draw value min max width)~, draws a bar in the cell with Org's 11-character gradient. Any other Lisp works too: ~'(identity $1)~ gets the field as a string (a number under ~N~, as written under ~L~), a range as the list of its strings, and ~'(org-lookup-first $1 '(remote(prices, @I$1..@>$1)) '(remote(prices, @I$2..@>$2)))~ looks a value up in another table; ~org-lookup-last~ and ~org-lookup-all~ are there too.

*** Plots
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: plots
:END:

A ~#+PLOT:~ line directly above a table (stacked lines combine) graphs its data. *📊 Plot* below the table shows the graph inline as SVG; tap again to hide it. The app reads org-plot's own options, so an unmodified line works. See =examples/plots.org=.

#+begin_example
#+PLOT: title:"Sales" ind:1 deps:(2 3) with:lines
| Month | Pens | Books |
|-------+------+-------|
| Jan   |   40 |    12 |
| Feb   |   55 |    18 |
#+end_example

~type:2d~ (the default) and ~type:radar~ are drawn; ~with:~ is ~lines~, ~points~, ~boxes~ (also ~histograms~) or ~impulses~.

| Option | Meaning |
|---+---|
| ~title~ | A quoted string |
| ~ind~ | The column for the x position (2d) or axis label (radar); without it the x position is the row number |
| ~deps~ | The columns to plot; default every column except ~ind~ (every column when there is no ~ind~) |
| ~labels~ | Quoted series names, by column number; default the header row |
| ~transpose~ | ~yes~ swaps rows and columns first (how a radar chart gets its axes) |
| ~min~, ~max~, ~xmin~, ~xmax~ | The y range, and the x range when ~ind~ is numeric |
| ~ticks~ | The number of y gridlines; default 5 |

Options that only script gnuplot (~set~, ~line~, ~script~, ~file~, ~map~, ~timefmt~) are accepted and ignored, so a copied line never errors. Editing the table re-renders the graph the next time it is shown.
